blocks.tx: Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Peptide / Oligopeptide (tripeptide).
**Size/Structure:** Composed of 3 amino acids.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Hypothalamus.
**Specific Cell Type / Nuclei:** Neurons in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus; secreted from nerve endings in the median eminence into the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Membrane-bound G-protein coupled receptor (Gαq) on target anterior pituitary cells.

**Signaling Pathway & Second Messengers:** Activates phospholipase C (PLC), which cleaves membrane phosphatidylinositols (PIP₂) to generate **inositol triphosphate (IP₃)** and **diacylglycerol (DAG)**.IP₃ triggers intracellularCa²⁺ release from the endoplasmic reticulum, while DAG activates protein kinase C. (Also utilizes cyclic AMP in general pituitary signaling contexts).
Target Tissues
Anterior pituitary gland (specifically thyrotrophs, lactotrophs, and somatotrophs).
Hypothalamic thermoregulatory pathways.
Functions
**Anterior Pituitary System:**
*Direct Effect on Thyrotrophs:* Stimulates the secretion of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH / thyrotropin) from thyrotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
*Direct Effect on Gene Expression:* Stimulates gene expression for both theα andβ subunits of TSH in thyrotrophs.
*Direct Effect on Lactotrophs:* Promotes the secretion of prolactin (PRL).
*Direct Effect on Somatotrophs:* Promotes the secretion of growth hormone (GH).
**Thermoregulatory / Metabolic System:**

*Indirect / Physiological Effect:* Cooling of the anterior hypothalamic-preoptic area increases TRH release, which via TSH and thyroxine output activates uncoupling proteins to increase cellular metabolism and heat production (chemical thermogenesis).
Regulation

**Negative Feedback (Long Loop):** Free triiodothyronine (T₃) and thyroxine (T₄) secreted by the thyroid gland inhibit TRH release from the hypothalamus as well as TSH release from the anterior pituitary.

**Hypothalamic Energy Sensing Loop:** TRH neurons in the PVN receive direct neural inputs from leptin-responsive arcuate nucleus neurons—specifically neuropeptide Y (NPY) / agouti-related protein (AGRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion / Expression:**
Exposure to cold (cooling of the anterior hypothalamic-preoptic area).
High plasma leptin levels (maintain POMC activity and suppress NPY/AGRP inhibition on TRH neurons).
**Factors Decreasing Secretion / Expression:**
Elevated circulatingT₃ andT₄ (negative feedback).
Prolonged fasting / starvation (decreases plasma leptin, decreasing POMC activity and increasing NPY/AGRP activity, which directly inhibits TRH neurons to reduce metabolic rate and conserve energy).
Emotional reactions such as excitement and anxiety (conditions that stimulate the sympathetic nervous system cause an acute decrease in TSH/TRH secretion).
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide.
**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 41 amino acids.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Hypothalamus.

**Specific Cell Type / Nuclei:** Neurons in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus; released at nerve terminals in the median eminence into the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vascular system.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Cell-surface G-protein coupled receptors on corticotropes in the anterior pituitary.
**Signaling Pathway & Second Messengers:** Activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular **cyclic AMP (cAMP)**, which triggers enzyme cascades regulating hormone synthesis and exocytosis.
Target Tissues
Anterior pituitary gland (corticotrophs).
Central nervous system / brainstem reticular activating system.
Sympathetic nervous system and cardiovascular system.
Functions
**Anterior Pituitary / Endocrine System:**
*Direct Action on Corticotrophs:* Stimulates the synthesis and secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH / corticotropin) from corticotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
*Direct Action on Gene Expression:* Stimulates the expression of the pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) gene in corticotrophs.
*Direct Action on Peptide Processing:* Promotes the secretion ofβ-lipotropin,γ-lipotropin, andβ-endorphins.
**Autonomic & Cardiovascular Systems:**
*Direct / Central Action:* Stimulates sympathetic nervous system activity.
*Systemic Effect:* Increases blood pressure.
**Central Nervous System:**
*Arousal Action:* Activates the brainstem reticular activating system, causing behavioral arousal.
*Stress Response Initiation:* Acts as the primary hypothalamic initiator of the hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) stress axis.
Regulation
**Negative Feedback Loops:**
*Long Loop:* Cortisol directly inhibits CRH secretion from the hypothalamus (and ACTH from the anterior pituitary).
*Short Loop:* ACTH directly inhibits CRH secretion from the hypothalamus.
*Ultrashort Loop:* CRH directly inhibits its own release from the hypothalamus.

**Stress Override:** Physical and psychological stress stimuli activate higher brain centers (e.g., limbic system/amygdala) to release CRH at a high rate, overriding the negative feedback inhibition of cortisol.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion:**
Physical stress (hypoglycemia, trauma, surgery, injury, infection, fever, anesthesia).
Psychological and emotional stress (anxiety, depression, fear).
Painful stimuli (via ascending nociceptive pathways sending collaterals to the hypothalamus).
Amygdaloid projections via the amygdalo-hypothalamic pathway.
Neurotransmitters/Neuropeptides: Norepinephrine (NE), Acetylcholine (ACh), 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT / Serotonin),α-receptor agonists,β-receptor antagonists, Interleukins, and GI hormones.
Sleep-wake transitions and circadian inputs (via suprachiasmatic nucleus and nucleus tractus solitarius / NTS).
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:**
Elevated circulating Cortisol.
Elevated ACTH.
Somatostatin.
GABA.
Brain Natriuretic Peptide (BNP).
Opioids.
CRH self-inhibition (ultrashort loop).
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide.
**Size/Structure:** Appears in two active forms in humans: a 40-amino acid chain and a 44-amino acid single chain.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Hypothalamus.

**Specific Cell Type / Nuclei:** Neurons in the arcuate nucleus and ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus; secreted at nerve endings in the median eminence into hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Cell membrane receptors on somatotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
**Signaling Pathway & Second Messengers:** Activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cytosolic **cAMP**, which promotes growth hormone synthesis and exocytosis.
Target Tissues
Anterior pituitary gland (somatotrophs).
Functions
**Anterior Pituitary / Somatotrophic System:**
*Direct Action on Secretion:* Stimulates the synthesis and secretion of human growth hormone (hGH / somatotropin) from somatotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
*Direct Action on Gene Expression:* Promotes GH synthesis by stimulating the transcription and expression of the *GH* gene in somatotrophs.
Regulation
**Dual Hypothalamic Control:** GH secretion is governed by the functional balance between stimulatory GHRH and inhibitory Growth Hormone-Inhibitory Hormone (Somatostatin).
**Negative Feedback Loop:**
GH exerts negative feedback on GHRH release while exerting positive feedback on somatostatin release.
Somatomedin C (IGF-1), produced in response to GH, exerts negative feedback directly on GHRH release in the hypothalamus and on somatotrophs in the anterior pituitary.
**Glucostat Integration:** GHRH-secreting neurons in the arcuate/ventromedial nuclei overlap with glucose-sensing centers that govern hunger and satiety, aligning GH release with nutritional state.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion / Action:**

*Metabolic/Nutritional:* Hypoglycemia (low blood glucose), low blood free fatty acids, elevated blood amino acids (especially arginine), starvation/fasting, severe protein deficiency (kwashiorkor), and ghrelin (secreted by the stomach before meals).
*Physiological/Environmental:* Physical exercise, deep sleep (stages II and IV / first 2 hours of deep sleep), excitement, trauma, and stress (fever, surgery, psychological trauma).
*Hormonal:* Estrogens, androgens, puberty.
*Pharmacological/Neurochemical:* L-dopa,α-adrenergic agonists, apomorphine, acetylcholine, serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, and enkephalins.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion / Action:**
*Metabolic/Nutritional:* Hyperglycemia (increased blood glucose), increased blood free fatty acids, obesity.
*Hormonal/Feedback:* Exogenous or endogenous GH, Somatomedins (IGF-1), Somatostatin, Cortisol, Medroxyprogesterone.
*Physiological/Age:* REM sleep, aging (GH/GHRH axis decreases slowly after adolescence to ~25% in old age), pregnancy.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Peptide / Polypeptide.
**Size/Structure:** Occurs in two active polypeptide forms: a **14-amino acid form (SS-14)** and a **28-amino acid form (SS-28)**. Single chain of 14 amino acids in the hypothalamic context.
Properties
**Half-Life:** Extremely short circulating half-life of approximately **3 minutes**.
Source
**Gland/Organ & Specific Cell Types:**
*Hypothalamus:* Neurons in the anterior periventricular nucleus / periventricular area (secretes into median eminence).
*Pancreas:*D cells of the islets of Langerhans (synthesizes predominantly SS-14).
*Gastrointestinal Tract:*D cells of the gastric, duodenal, and intestinal mucosa from stomach to colon (synthesizes predominantly SS-28).
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Membrane G-protein coupled receptors on target cells.

**Signaling Pathway:** Inhibitory G-protein (G_i) linkage that suppresses adenylyl cyclase, decreases cAMP levels, and modulates intracellular ion channels via neurocrine, paracrine, and endocrine pathways.
Target Tissues
Anterior pituitary gland (somatotrophs, thyrotrophs, lactotrophs).
Pancreatic Islets of Langerhans (α cells andβ cells).
Gastrointestinal tract (G cells, parietal cells, mucosal epithelial cells, gallbladder, stomach, and intestine).
Central Nervous System.
Functions
**Anterior Pituitary / Endocrine System (Direct Actions):**
*Somatotrophs:* Inhibits the synthesis and secretion of Growth Hormone (GH).
*Somatotroph Gene Expression:* Inhibits *GH* gene transcription in somatotrophs.
*Thyrotrophs:* Inhibits the secretion of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH).
*Lactotrophs:* Inhibits the secretion of Prolactin (PRL).
*Corticotrophs:* Inhibits ACTH secretion.
**Pancreatic Islets (Paracrine / Local Actions):**
*Beta Cells:* Depresses insulin secretion locally within the islets.
*Alpha Cells:* Depresses glucagon secretion locally within the islets.
**Gastrointestinal System (Direct Actions):**
*G Cells:* Inhibits gastrin secretion from gastricD cells/mucosa (especially when luminalpH < 2).
*Gastric Parietal Cells:* InhibitsHCl secretion directly and indirectly (via gastrin suppression).
*Gastric Chief Cells:* Inhibits pepsin secretion.
*Other GI Peptides:* Inhibits secretion of VIP, GIP, Secretin, and Motilin.
*Pancreatic Exocrine:* Inhibits pancreatic exocrine digestive enzyme and fluid secretion.
*Motility:* Decreases motility of the stomach, duodenum, and gallbladder; inhibits gastric emptying when food enters the intestine to prevent rapid intestinal overload.

*Assimilation & Absorption:* Inhibits absorption of glucose, triglycerides, and other nutrients from intestinal mucosal epithelial cells; decreases overall GI secretion and absorption to extend the period over which food nutrients are assimilated into the blood.
**Central Nervous System:**
*Neurotransmission:* Acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in multiple brain regions, particularly the hypothalamus and pituitary.
Types
**SS-14 (14 Amino Acids):** Synthesized primarily in the hypothalamus and pancreaticD cells.
**SS-28 (28 Amino Acids):** Synthesized primarily in the mucosalD cells of the gastrointestinal tract.
Regulation
**Stimuli Increasing Secretion:**
*Endocrine/Feedback:* Elevated GH, elevated IGF-1 (Somatomedin C), and elevated Prolactin (positive feedback loops).
*Ingestion of Food / Luminal Factors:* Increased blood glucose, increased amino acids, increased fatty acids, and upper GI hormones released during food intake.
*Gastric pH:* Decreased pH of gastric content (pH < 2) directly stimulates gastricD cells to secrete somatostatin (autoregulation of acid secretion).
*Autonomic:* Vagal (cholinergic) stimulation and sympathetic stimulation viaβ-adrenergic receptors.
Clinical Correlates
**Therapeutic Uses:** Synthetic somatostatin preparations are used clinically to treat severe diarrhea due to its potent inhibition of GI motility, blood flow, and fluid secretion.
**Pathological States:** *Somatostatinoma* (D-cell tumor of the pancreas).
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Peptide / Decapeptide.
**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 10 amino acids.
**Exact Amino Acid Formula:**Glu - His - Trp - Ser - Tyr - Gly - Leu - Arg - Pro - Gly - NH₂.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Hypothalamus.

**Specific Cell Type / Nuclei:** Neurons with cell bodies located in the arcuate nuclei (mediobasal hypothalamus) and preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus; nerve terminals end in the median eminence.
Secretion
**Pattern:** Intermittent, **pulsatile secretion** occurring in short bursts lasting 5 to 25 minutes every 1 to 3 hours (\approxevery 90minutes).
**Mechanism & Portal Transport:** Released into the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vascular system to reach anterior pituitary gonadotropes.

**Critical Pulsatility Requirement:** Continuous (non-pulsatile) exposure to GnRH causes total loss of LH and FSH release due to receptor down-regulation on gonadotropes. Pulsatile release is absolute for maintaining gonadotrope sensitivity and function.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Plasma membrane G-protein coupled receptors on gonadotropes of the anterior pituitary.
**Down-Regulation Mechanism:** Chronic continuous receptor occupancy causes receptor internalization/down-regulation, suppressing LH/FSH synthesis and release.
Target Tissues
Anterior pituitary gland (gonadotropes).
Functions
**Anterior Pituitary / Gonadotropic System:**
*Direct Action on LH:* Stimulates the synthesis and pulsatile release of Luteinizing Hormone (LH / LHRH) from gonadotropes.
*Direct Action on FSH:* Stimulates the synthesis and release of Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) from gonadotropes.
*Direct Action on Somatotrophs:* Promotes secretion of Growth Hormone (GH).
**Reproductive System (Indirect Actions via LH/FSH):**
*Pubertal & Gametogenic Function:* Essential for attaining reproductive capability, pubertal maturation, spermatogenesis in males, and follicular development/ovulation in females.
*Steroidogenesis:* Drives testicular production of testosterone (via LH on Leydig cells) and ovarian production of estrogens/progestins (via LH/FSH on theca/granulosa cells).
Regulation
**Hypothalamic Pulse Generator:** Located in the arcuate nuclei of the mediobasal hypothalamus.
**Feedback Regulation by Sex Steroids & Peptides:**
*Negative Feedback:* Testosterone, Progesterone, Androgens, and Inhibin (from Sertoli/granulosa cells and corpus luteum) suppress GnRH pulse frequency and/or secretion.

*Positive Feedback (Preovulatory LH Surge):* High sustained levels of Estrogen towards the end of the female follicular phase increase GnRH burst frequency and increase gonadotrope sensitivity, triggering the preovulatory LH surge required for ovulation.
*Prolactin Inhibition:* Elevated prolactin directly inhibits hypothalamic GnRH secretion (causing hypogonadism/amenorrhea).
**Neural / Neurochemical Control:**
*Norepinephrine (NE):* Stimulates GnRH release.
*Dopamine, Endorphins, and Enkephalins:* Inhibit GnRH release and reduce pulse frequency.
*Limbic System:* Transmits psychic and emotional signals into arcuate nuclei, altering pulse frequency and intensity.
Factors Affecting
**Childhood Suppression:** During childhood, the hypothalamus does not secrete significant GnRH despite being capable, keeping the pituitary-gonadal axis dormant until puberty.
Clinical Correlates

**Therapeutic Uses (Long-Acting GnRH Analogs):** Synthetic long-acting GnRH analogs (administered continuously) are used to treat **precocious puberty** and **prostate cancer**. Continuous exposure down-regulates gonadotrope receptors, selectively suppressing LH and sex steroid production.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Catecholamine / Amine hormone (derived from the amino acid tyrosine; 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine).
**Size/Structure:** Small organic amine molecule (not a peptide).
Properties
**Solubility & Storage:** Amine hormone stored in secretory granules within dopaminergic nerve terminals; released by calcium-mediated exocytosis.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Hypothalamus.

**Specific Cell Type / Nuclei:** Tuberoinfundibular dopaminergic neurons with cell bodies located in the arcuate nuclei and periventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus; nerve fibers terminate in the median eminence.
Secretion
**Dominant Tonal Pattern:** Unlike other hypothalamic factors that are primarily releasing hormones, dopamine exerts **continuous, baseline tonic inhibition** over prolactin secretion.

**Portal Transport:** Secreted into the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels to reach lactotrophs. Interrupting the portal system (e.g., pituitary stalk transection or hypothalamic damage) removes this inhibition and increases prolactin secretion up to 10-fold while depressing other anterior pituitary hormones.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Types & Subtypes:** Membrane-bound dopaminergic receptors (D₁, D₂, D₃, D₄, D₅).

**Lactotroph Mechanism:** Inhibition of prolactin synthesis and exocytosis in lactotrophs is mediated primarily through **D₂ receptors**, which couple to inhibitory G-proteins (G_i) to decrease intracellular cAMP and reduce intracellular calcium.
Target Tissues
Anterior pituitary gland (lactotrophs, thyrotrophs, somatotrophs).
Central Nervous System (basal ganglia / neostriatum, limbic system).
Functions
**Anterior Pituitary / Endocrine System (Direct Actions):**
*Lactotrophs:* Inhibits both the synthesis and secretion of Prolactin (PRL) from lactotrophs (can decrease prolactin secretion up to 10-fold).
*Thyrotrophs:* Inhibits Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) secretion.
*Somatotrophs:* Inhibits Growth Hormone (GH) secretion.
*Gonadotropic Axis:* Inhibits hypothalamic GnRH release.
**Central Nervous System / Motor & Neuroendocrine Systems:**

*Nigrostriatal System:* Dopamine released from the pars compacta of substantia nigra to the neostriatum (caudate and putamen) is essential for maintaining normal muscle tone, posture, and voluntary movements.
*Basal Ganglia Co-transmission:* Acts as a co-transmitter with Substance P in the basal ganglia.
*Tuberoinfundibular System:* Controls hypothalamic releasing factor secretion into the portal system.
Regulation

**Short-Loop Negative Feedback:** Prolactin stimulates hypothalamic dopaminergic neurons to increase dopamine synthesis and release, which in turn acts on lactotrophs to suppress further prolactin secretion.

**Suckling / Lactation Reflex:** Infant suckling on the nipple stimulates mechanoreceptors, sending sensory impulses up the spinal cord to the hypothalamus that **inhibit dopamine release**. The resulting drop in dopamine removes lactotroph inhibition, triggering episodic bursts of prolactin required for lactogenesis.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Dopamine Action (Suppressing Prolactin):**
Dopamine, Dopamine Agonists (e.g., bromocriptine, cabergoline), GABA, and Prolactin itself (via short-loop feedback).
**Factors Decreasing Dopamine Release or Blocking Action (Increasing Prolactin):**
Breastfeeding / Suckling reflex (nipple mechanoreceptor stimulation).
Psychological stress, sleep, pregnancy, and high-dose estrogen therapy.
Neuropeptides/Hormones: TRH, PRF, Oxytocin, Angiotensin II, Serotonin, and Opioids.
PharmacologicalD₂ receptor antagonists (e.g., antipsychotics), which blockD₂ receptors on lactotrophs and cause hyperprolactinemia.
Clinical Correlates

**Therapeutic Uses of Dopamine Agonists:** Dopaminergic drugs (e.g., bromocriptine) are used to treat **hyperprolactinemia**, **prolactin-secreting tumors (prolactinomas/lactotroph adenomas)**, and **amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome**. Suppressing prolactin restores normal GnRH, LH/FSH secretion, fertility, and libido.
**Drug-Induced Hyperprolactinemia:**D₂ receptor antagonists block dopamine action on lactotrophs, leading to elevated prolactin levels, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility.
Summary Comparison Table
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Hypothalamus.
**Specific Cell Type:** Source within the hypothalamus is not exactly known.
Target Tissues
Anterior pituitary gland (lactotrophs).
Functions
**Anterior Pituitary System:**
*Direct Effect on Lactotrophs:* Stimulates prolactin (PRL) synthesis and secretion from lactotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
Regulation
**Negative Feedback Loop:** Prolactin inhibits its own secretion by stimulating hypothalamic release of dopamine and somatostatin, which suppress lactotroph activity.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Action / Release:**
Pregnancy, estrogen therapy, nursing (breastfeeding), sleep, stress, angiotensin II, oxytocin, dopamine antagonists, serotonin, and opioids promote prolactin secretion (partly via PRF action).
A. Ghrelin
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide.
**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 28 amino acids.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Secreted mainly from the stomach; also listed among hypothalamic / gastrointestinal peptides.
Target Tissues
Arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
Anterior pituitary gland (somatotrophs).
Functions
**Feeding & Metabolic System:**
*Direct Central Effect:* Acts as a potent orexigenic agent that increases food intake by acting on the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
**Anterior Pituitary / Somatotrophic System:**
*Direct Endocrine Effect:* Stimulates the secretion of growth hormone (GH) from somatotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
Factors Affecting
Secreted by the stomach before meals (hunger state).
B. Orexins (Orexin-A and Orexin-B / Hypocretin)
Source
**Gland/Organ & Nuclei:** Synthesized by neurons in the lateral hypothalamus and zona incerta.
Target Tissues
Widespread brain regions containing orexin receptors.
Functions
**Feeding & Energy Homeostasis System:**
*Direct Central Effect:* Acts as orexigenic neurotransmitters to stimulate food intake.
**Central Nervous System / Sleep-Wake Regulation:**

*Arousal & Vigilance:* Provide excitatory input to many areas of the brain to promote arousal and maintain wakefulness. Orexin neurons are most active during waking and almost stop firing during slow-wave and REM sleep.
Types
**Orexin-A** and **Orexin-B** (also termed hypocretins).
Clinical Correlates

**Deficiency State:** Loss of orexin signaling resulting from defective orexin receptors or destruction of orexin-producing neurons causes **narcolepsy** (a sleep disorder characterized by overwhelming daytime drowsiness and sudden sleep attacks) and **cataplexy** (sudden loss of muscle tone leading to partial or total paralysis during attacks).
C. Cocaine- and Amphetamine-Regulated Transcript (CART)
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Hypothalamus.
Target Tissues
Hypothalamic feeding centers.
Functions
**Feeding System:**
*Anorexigenic Effect:* Inhibits food intake and decreases appetite.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide / Protein.
**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 191 amino acids; molecular weight of 22,005 (or 22,000 for the 22 K form). Displays structural resemblance to human prolactin and human placental lactogen.
Properties
**Half-Life:** Rapidly metabolized; half-life is approximately **6 to 20 minutes**.
**Basal Plasma Concentration:** 0–5 ng/ml (or < 3 ng/ml under resting adult conditions).
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Anterior pituitary gland.
**Specific Cell Type:** Somatotrophs (constitute about 50% of the total endocrine cell population of the anterior pituitary).
Synthesis
**Key Steps & Processing:**
Synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum as a larger **prohormone** containing an N-terminal signal peptide attached to the 191-amino acid peptide chain.
The signal peptide is removed as the prohormone traverses the Golgi apparatus.
The active 191-amino acid hormone is packaged and stored in secretory granules within somatotrophs.

**Gene Expression Factors:** Expression of the *GH* gene in somatotrophs is directly promoted by hypothalamic GHRH and by Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH). *(Discrepancy Note: One source notes that TSH stimulates GH gene expression, causing patients with thyroid hormone gene deficiency to develop concurrent GH deficiency).*
Secretion
**Pattern:** Pulsatile secretion with marked 24-hour diurnal fluctuations; approximately two-thirds (70%) of total daily GH secretion occurs during slow-wave sleep (stages 3 and 4 / around midnight).
**Mechanism:** Exocytosis of stored secretory granules driven by GHRH stimulation.
Transport
**Bound Fraction:** Approximately 50% of circulating GH is bound to a specific plasma protein—a fragment of the extracellular domain of the GH receptor. This bound pool serves as a plasma reservoir.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Cell membrane-bound polypeptide receptor containing 620 amino acids; belongs to the cytokine receptor superfamily (tyrosine kinase-associated receptor).

**Structure & Dimerization:** Consists of three domains (extracellular, transmembrane, and cytoplasmic) with two subunits. GH binding to one subunit attracts the second subunit, inducing **receptor dimerization**, which activates the intracellular tyrosine kinase **Janus kinase 2 (JAK2)**.
**Signaling Pathways:**

*JAK-STAT Pathway:* JAK2 phosphorylates STATs (Signal Transducers and Activators of Transcription), which translocate to the nucleus to bind response elements (SIE, SRE, GLE-1, GLE-2) and induce transcription of target genes.
*SHC-Grb-MAPK Pathway:* JAK2 phosphorylates SHC, activating Grb2 and MAP-kinase to induce gene transcription.
*TK-IRS Pathway:* JAK2 phosphorylates Insulin Receptor Substrate (IRS) to activate downstream intracellular enzymes.
*Phospholipase-C Pathway:* Activates membrane Phospholipase C to form Diacylglycerol (DAG), triggering intracellularCa²⁺ influx and activating Protein Kinase C.
Target Tissues

Direct actions on virtually all growing tissues of the body: epiphyseal cartilage/chondrocytes, bone (osteoblasts and osteoclasts), skeletal muscle, visceral organs (liver, kidney, heart, pancreas, intestine), adipose tissue, skin, connective tissue, and gonads.
Indirect actions via the liver (production of IGF-1 / Somatomedin C).
Functions
**Protein & Anabolic System (Direct Actions):**
*Amino Acid Uptake & Translation:* Enhances amino acid transport across cell membranes and promotes RNA translation by cytoplasmic ribosomes.
*Transcription:* Increases nuclear DNA transcription to form mRNA over prolonged periods (24–48 hours).
*Protein Sparing:* Decreases catabolism of proteins and amino acids by shifting cellular energy utilization toward free fatty acids.
*Skeletal Muscle:* Stimulates muscle growth by promoting protein synthesis, inducing muscle cell hypertrophy, and increasing the proliferation of progenitor satellite cells.

*Visceral Organs & Tissues:* Stimulates growth, hypertrophy, and hyperplasia of the liver, kidneys, heart, pancreas, intestines, endocrine glands, skin, and connective tissue, enhancing both their size and organ-specific functions (e.g., improves digestion, increases cardiac output and GFR).
**Metabolic System (Direct Acute Actions):**

*Lipid Metabolism:* Mobilizes free fatty acids from adipose tissue into body fluids (lipolysis); enhances conversion of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA and their utilization for energy in preference to carbohydrates and proteins.
*Ketogenic Effect (Dose-Dependent/Excess):* Under excessive GH levels, extreme fat mobilization leads to large acetoacetic acid production by the liver, causing ketosis and fatty liver.

*Carbohydrate Metabolism (Diabetogenic / Anti-Insulin Action):* Causes "insulin resistance" by decreasing glucose uptake and utilization in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, increasing hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis), and secondary compensatory insulin hypersecretion.
**Skeletal & Cartilage System (Direct & Indirect Actions via IGF-1):**

*Epiphyseal Linear Growth (Direct on Chondrocytes):* Facilitates differentiation of progenitor prechondrocytes into chondrocytes in bone growth plates; increases chondrocyte size and proliferation; promotes incorporation of proline into collagen (converted to hydroxyproline) and sulfate into chondroitin, building the extracellular cartilage matrix and increasing long bone length before epiphyseal fusion.
*Bone Modeling & Mass (Direct on Bone):* Stimulates both osteoblasts and osteoclasts (osteoblastic activity predominates), increasing total bone mass and mineral content.
*Membranous Bone Growth:* Continuously stimulates osteoblasts in bone periosteum throughout life, increasing the thickness of membranous bones (e.g., jaw, skull, nose, suprabulbar ridges).
**Renal & Electrolyte System (Direct Actions):**
*Sodium & Water Retention:* DecreasesNa⁺ and water excretion by stimulating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and suppressing the action of Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) on the kidneys.
*Phosphate Balance:* Increases plasma phosphate levels by enhancing its reabsorption in renal proximal tubules.
**Reproductive System (Direct Actions):**
*Pubertal Growth:* Drives the pubertal height spurt.

*Gametogenesis:* Controls background metabolic functions of the testes; directly promotes early mitotic division of spermatogonia (in GH deficiency, spermatogenesis is severely deficient or absent, causing male infertility).
**Indirect Actions (Mediated via IGF-1 / Somatomedin C from Liver):**

*Somatic & Cartilage Growth:* Mediates linear epiphyseal growth, visceral enlargement, protein deposition, and prevents lipolysis while displaying insulin-like activity. *(Note: IGF-II is independent of GH action and mediates fetal growth).*
Types / Isoforms
**22 K GH:** Molecular weight 22,000; accounts for **90%** of total circulating GH.
**20 K GH:** Molecular weight 20,000; accounts for **10%** of total circulating GH.
**hGH:** Recombinant human growth hormone synthesized by *E. coli* for therapeutic use.
Regulation
**Dual Hypothalamic Axis:** Governed by stimulatory GHRH and inhibitory Somatostatin (GHIH).
**Feedback Loops:**
*Negative Feedback:* Exogenous/endogenous GH and IGF-1 inhibit GHRH release and stimulate somatostatin release from the hypothalamus; GH directly inhibits its own secretion.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion:**
*Metabolic/Nutritional:* Hypoglycemia, low blood free fatty acids, high blood amino acids (especially arginine), starvation/fasting, severe protein deficiency (kwashiorkor), and ghrelin.
*Physiological/Environmental:* Physical exercise, slow-wave deep sleep (stages 3 and 4), excitement, trauma, fever, surgery, psychological stress, puberty, estrogens, and androgens.
*Pharmacological:* L-dopa,α-adrenergic agonists, dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, acetylcholine, and enkephalins.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:**
*Metabolic/Nutritional:* Hyperglycemia, elevated blood free fatty acids, obesity.
*Hormonal/Feedback:* Exogenous GH, IGFs, Somatostatin, Cortisol, Medroxyprogesterone.
*Physiological/Age:* REM sleep, aging (GH secretion declines post-adolescence to ~25% in old age), and pregnancy.
Metabolism and Clearance
Rapidly degraded in the liver. Half-life is 6 to 20 minutes. A small fraction is excreted unchanged in urine (24-hour urinary GH reflects daily secretory output).
Clinical Correlates
**Hypersecretion States:**

**Gigantism (Pre-pubertal / Before Epiphyseal Fusion):** Caused by somatotroph adenomas or GHRH-secreting tumors during childhood. *Features:* Extreme height (up to 8 feet), rapid soft tissue/visceral growth, large hands/feet, hyperglycemia/full-blown diabetes mellitus (~10% of patients due to beta-cell exhaustion), and eventual panhypopituitarism if tumor growth destroys the pituitary gland.

**Acromegaly (Post-pubertal / After Epiphyseal Fusion):** Caused by somatotroph adenomas (co-secrete prolactin in 20–40% of cases) or extra-pituitary GHRH tumors. *Features:* Enlargement of acral parts (broadened hands, feet, fingers), acromegalic facies (frontal bossing, enlarged nose/lips/tongue, prognathism/malocclusion), osteoarthritic skeletal deformities, visceromegaly (cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly, nephromegaly, splenomegaly), hypertension, skin tags, hyperhidrosis, carpal tunnel syndrome, bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm compression), headaches, and galactorrhea.
**Deficiency States:**

**Pituitary Dwarfism (Childhood Deficiency):** Short stature with delayed bone and sexual maturation. Features include decreased muscle mass, reduced bone density, and decreased cardiac function. *Mental development remains normal* (distinguishing it from thyroid dwarfism).
**Laron Dwarfism / African Pygmies:** GH levels are normal or high, but responsiveness is absent due to GH receptor mutations (Laron) or a hereditary inability to synthesize IGF-1 (African pygmies).
**Diagnostic Tests:** High plasma GH levels, low plasma IGF-1 levels, 24-hour urinary GH, and CT/MRI of the sella turcica.
**Therapeutic Uses:** Recombinant human GH (hGH) completely cures pure GH deficiency if initiated early in life.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Glycoprotein.
**Size/Structure:** Molecular weight of approximately 28,000. Dimeric molecule consisting of two non-covalently linked subunits (α andβ):
**α Subunit:** Non-specific; contains 96 amino acids and shares an identical amino acid sequence with LH, FSH, and hCG.
**β Subunit:** Specific; contains 110 amino acids and confers biological specificity.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Anterior pituitary gland.
**Specific Cell Type:** Thyrotrophs.
Synthesis
**Processing Steps:**
Synthesized as a preprohormone and processed to a prohormone.
Theα andβ peptide chains are translated separately from distinct mRNA molecules.
Chains undergo glycosylation in the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
During packaging in the Golgi apparatus, carbohydrate moieties are modified by adding sialic acid and sulfate, allowing theα andβ subunits to assemble into the functional TSH dimer.
Secretion
**Plasma Concentration:** Normal basal level is **0.3 to 5\muU/ml**.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Cell-surface receptors on the basolateral membrane of thyroid follicular epithelial cells.
**Signaling Pathway & Second Messenger:** Activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cytosolic **cyclic AMP (cAMP)**, which triggers protein kinase cascades and rapid/long-term cellular responses.
Target Tissues
Thyroid gland (follicular epithelial cells).
Anterior pituitary gland (somatotrophs).
Functions
**Thyroid Gland (Direct Secretory & Metabolic Actions):**
*Proteolysis of Thyroglobulin:* Initiates proteolysis of stored colloid thyroglobulin, releasingT₃ andT₄ into circulation within 30 minutes (the most immediate early effect).
*Iodide Trapping:* Increases sodium-iodide symporter (Na⁺-I⁻ symporter) activity on basolateral membranes, enhancing active iodide uptake.
*Iodination & Coupling:* Increases thyroid peroxidase-mediated iodination of tyrosine residues and coupling of iodotyrosines within thyroglobulin.
*Colloid Endocytosis:* Promotes pseudopod formation and endocytosis of colloid droplets from the follicular lumen.
*Thyroglobulin Synthesis:* Stimulates synthesis and exocytosis of thyroglobulin into the follicle lumen.
*Vascularity:* Increases blood flow through the thyroid gland.

*Glandular Hypertrophy & Hyperplasia:* Increases the size, number, and metabolic activity of thyroid follicular cells, transforming their morphology from flat/cuboidal to columnar with extensive luminal epithelial infoldings.
**Anterior Pituitary System:**
*Gene Expression:* Directly stimulates the expression of the *GH* gene in somatotrophs.
Regulation
**Hypothalamic Driving & Inhibitory Factors:** Secretion is stimulated by hypothalamic TRH and inhibited by hypothalamic Somatostatin and Dopamine.

**Negative Feedback Loop:** Free triiodothyronine (T₃) and thyroxine (T₄) secreted by the thyroid gland exert negative feedback on anterior pituitary thyrotrophs (suppressing TSH release) and hypothalamic PVN neurons (suppressing TRH release).
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion:** Hypothalamic TRH, cold exposure, decreased circulating freeT₃/T₄.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Elevated circulatingT₃/T₄, Somatostatin, Dopamine, Cortisol, Growth Hormone, prolonged fasting, and acute emotional stress/excitement.
Clinical Correlates
**Secondary Hypothyroidism (Hypopituitary):** Pituitary disease leads to deficient TSH, causing thyroid atrophy and low circulatingT₃/T₄.

**Primary Hypothyroidism:** Loss of thyroid hormone negative feedback causes high plasma TSH levels. Chronic TSH elevation produces diffuse enlargement and hypertrophy of the thyroid gland (**goiter**). *Diagnostic thresholds:* Subclinical hypothyroidism (5–10 \muU/ml); Clinical hypothyroidism (>10 \muU/ml).
**Primary Hyperthyroidism:** High circulatingT₃/T₄ levels suppress plasma TSH to low or undetectable levels.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Peptide.

**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 39 amino acids (the smallest anterior pituitary peptide hormone). Contains theα-MSH sequence at its N-terminal (amino acids 1–13), conferring intrinsicα-MSH activity.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Anterior pituitary gland (corticotrophs). Also expressed in the GI tract and brain.
Synthesis
**Precursor Molecule & Processing:**
Synthesized as part of a large preprohormone precursor named **Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)**.

Cleavage of POMC by prohormone convertase 1 (PC1) in corticotrophs yields **ACTH** and **β-lipotropin** (as well as N-terminal protein, joining protein,γ-MSH,γ-lipotropin,β-endorphin,α-MSH, and CLIP).
Secretion

**Pattern:** Distinct **circadian / diurnal rhythm**, with peak secretory bursts in the early morning (between 4 AM and 10 AM, an hour after waking) and a nadir around midnight. Pattern is reversed in individuals who sleep during the day.
**Stress Response:** Rapid, immediate surge in response to acute physical or psychological stress.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Cell membrane receptors on adrenocortical cells (zona fasciculata, zona reticularis, zona glomerulosa), skin melanocytes, lymphocytes, GI tract, and brain.

**Signaling Pathway & Second Messenger:** Activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cytosolic **cAMP** (maximal effect within 3 minutes), which activates protein kinases to stimulate adrenocortical steroidogenesis.
Target Tissues
Adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata, zona reticularis, and zona glomerulosa).
Skin melanocytes.
Immune system (lymphocytes).
Central Nervous System and Gastrointestinal Tract.
Functions
**Adrenocortical System (Direct Endocrine Actions):**
*Glucocorticoid & Androgen Steroidogenesis:* Stimulates the synthesis and secretion of cortisol and adrenal androgens (DHEA, androstenedione) from the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.
*Mineralocorticoid Secretion:* Temporarily stimulates aldosterone synthesis in the zona glomerulosa (requires higher ACTH concentrations than cortisol; effect is transient).
*Trophic Effect:* Promotes growth, structural maintenance, hypertrophy, and cellular proliferation of the adrenal cortex (particularly zona fasciculata and reticularis).
**Integumentary System (Direct Actions via Intrinsic MSH Activity):**
*Melanocyte Activation:* Stimulates growth and melanin synthesis in skin melanocytes via its N-terminalα-MSH sequence, producing skin hyperpigmentation when plasma ACTH levels are high.
**Immune System:**
*Cytokine Modulation:* Controls cytokine secretion from lymphocytes (cytokines also reciprocally stimulate ACTH secretion).
**Central Nervous System & GI Tract:**
*Neurotransmission:* Functions as a local neurotransmitter in central and gastrointestinal neural networks.
Regulation
**Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) Axis:** Driven primarily by hypothalamic Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH) and Vasopressin (ADH).
**Negative Feedback Loops:**
*Long Loop:* Cortisol directly inhibits ACTH release from corticotrophs and CRH from the hypothalamus.
*Short Loop:* ACTH directly inhibits CRH release from the hypothalamus.

**Stress Override:** Stress stimuli trigger higher brain centers to stimulate CRH release at high rates, overriding cortisol negative feedback and establishing a higher secretory setpoint during chronic stress.
Factors Affecting

**Factors Increasing Secretion:** CRH, ADH, sleep-wake transitions, physical stress (hypoglycemia, surgery, trauma, injury, infection, fever, anesthesia), anxiety, depression,α-adrenergic agonists,β-blockers, serotonin, acetylcholine, interleukins, and GI hormones.

**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Cortisol, ACTH, Somatostatin, GABA, Brain Natriuretic Peptide (BNP), opioids, and prolonged high-dose glucocorticoid therapy (suppresses the axis for up to 10 months post-withdrawal).
Clinical Correlates
**Excess States:**
**Cushing's Disease:** ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma causing bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and hypercortisolism.
**Hyperpigmentation:** Seen in Addison's disease (loss of adrenal cortisol negative feedback causes compensatory ACTH/POMC hypersecretion) and ACTH-secreting pituitary tumors.
**Deficiency States:** Secondary adrenocortical insufficiency (adrenal atrophy) resulting from hypopituitarism or abrupt withdrawal of chronic glucocorticoid therapy.
**Diagnostic Tests:** Diurnal plasma ACTH measurements, Short/Long Dexamethasone Suppression Tests (SDAST / LDAST), and Low-Dose ACTH Stimulation Test.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Glycoprotein.
**Size/Structure:** Molecular weight of approximately 30,000. Heterodimeric glycoprotein consisting of two subunits:
**α Subunit:** Shared with LH, TSH, and hCG.
**β Subunit:** Specific to FSH, conferring receptor-binding specificity.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Anterior pituitary gland.
**Specific Cell Type:** Gonadotrophs (constitute 10–15% of the anterior pituitary cell population).
Secretion

**Pattern:** Pulsatile secretion driven by hypothalamic GnRH pulses. Displays cyclic fluctuations during the female monthly menstrual cycle (moderate increase during the early follicular phase, peaking before a midcycle surge). Secretion is extremely low during childhood, increases at puberty, and rises abruptly following menopause.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Specific cell-membrane FSH receptors located on ovarian target cells (granulosa cells) and testicular target cells (Sertoli cells).

**Signaling Pathway & Second Messenger:** Activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cytosolic **cAMP**, which activates protein kinases to induce multiple enzyme phosphorylations and specific gene transcription.
Target Tissues
Female: Ovaries (granulosa cells of developing follicles).
Male: Testes (Sertoli cells of seminiferous tubules).
Functions
**Female Reproductive System (Ovarian Folliculogenesis & Steroidogenesis):**

*Follicular Growth:* Controls early and antral folliculogenesis. Stimulates primary and secondary follicles to progress into tertiary/Graafian follicles by driving rapid granulosa cell proliferation, theca layer formation, and antral fluid accumulation. *(Note: Primordial follicle growth is gonadotropin-independent, but subsequent growth requires FSH).*

*Aromatase Induction & Estrogen Synthesis:* Acts on granulosa cells to stimulate **aromatase (CYP19)** enzyme activity, converting theca-derived androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) into estrogens (estradiol).

*Receptor Upregulation:* Stimulates granulosa cells to form increasing numbers of FSH receptors (positive feedback) and, in combination with estrogen, induces **LH receptors** on granulosa cells in late tertiary follicles.
*Inhibin-B Production:* Stimulates granulosa cells to synthesize and secrete **inhibin-B**.
*Ovulatory Support:* Stimulates plasminogen activator synthesis in granulosa cells, generating plasmin to break down the follicular wall and facilitate ovulatory rupture.
**Male Reproductive System (Testicular Gametogenesis & Sertoli Function):**
*Spermatogenesis:* Binds to Sertoli cells to initiate and maintain gametogenesis (essential alongside testosterone for converting spermatids to mature spermatozoa during spermiogenesis).

*Androgen-Binding Protein (ABP) Synthesis:* Increases cAMP in Sertoli cells to induce synthesis of ABP, which binds testosterone to maintain high local androgen concentrations within seminiferous tubules.

*Nutritional & Proteolytic Support:* Induces Sertoli cell synthesis of **transferrin** (iron transport protein for nourishing developing spermatids) and **plasminogen activator** (promotes spermiation / mature sperm detachment).
*Inhibin-B Secretion:* Stimulates Sertoli cells to synthesize and secrete **inhibin-B**.
Regulation
**Hypothalamic Control:** Driven by pulsatile Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH).
**Feedback Control:**
*Inhibin-B (Negative Feedback):* Secreted by granulosa cells in females and Sertoli cells in males; selectively suppresses FSH synthesis and secretion from anterior pituitary gonadotrophs.
*Activin (Positive Drive):* Produced in Sertoli/granulosa cells; directly stimulates FSH synthesis and secretion.
*Follistatin (Inhibition):* Binds and inactivates activin, indirectly suppressing FSH release.
*Sex Steroid Negative Feedback:* Estrogen and progesterone (females) or testosterone (males) suppress GnRH and FSH release.
*Prolactin Inhibition:* Elevated prolactin suppresses GnRH, secondarily depressing FSH.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion:** GnRH bursts, Activin, Menopause (abrupt loss of ovarian estrogen and inhibin-B feedback).

**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Inhibin-B, Follistatin, Estrogen, Progesterone, Testosterone, Prolactin, pre-pubertal childhood state, and continuous GnRH exposure (down-regulates gonadotrope receptors).
Clinical Correlates
**Deficiency States:**

**Kallmann's Syndrome:** Deficiency of GnRH neurons due to failure of migration from the olfactory bulb→ low GnRH, low FSH and LH→ hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, failure of pubertal maturation, infertility, and anosmia.
**Receptor Resistance:**
**FSH Resistance:** Caused by decreased number or sensitivity of FSH receptors on granulosa cells.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Glycoprotein hormone.

**Size/Structure:** Dimeric molecule composed of two non-covalently linked subunits: an alpha subunit and a beta subunit. The alpha subunit contains 96 amino acids and is non-specific (sharing identical amino acid sequence with FSH, TSH, and hCG), whereas the beta subunit provides biological specificity.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Anterior pituitary gland.
**Specific Cell Type:** Gonadotrophs (constitute 10–15% of the total anterior pituitary cell population).
Secretion
**Pattern:** Secreted in circhoral (episodic) bursts occurring every 30–60 minutes driven by episodic bursts of hypothalamic GnRH.
**Midcycle Surge:** Shortly before ovulation (24–48 hours before), secretion increases abruptly 6- to 10-fold, peaking about 8–16 hours before ovulation (the pre-ovulatory LH surge).
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Luteinizing Hormone Receptors (LHR) located on cell membranes of ovarian theca cells, granulosa cells, and luteal cells, as well as testicular Leydig cells.
**Signaling Pathway & Second Messenger:** Activates adenylyl cyclase to increase cytosolic cyclic AMP (cAMP).
Target Tissues
Female: Ovaries (theca cells, granulosa cells, luteal cells).
Male: Testes (Leydig cells / interstitial cells).
Functions
**Female Reproductive System (Ovarian Steroidogenesis, Ovulation, and Luteinization):**

*Theca Cell Androgen Synthesis (Direct Action):* Stimulates theca cells of developing ovarian follicles to synthesize and secrete androgens (androstenedione and testosterone), which diffuse into neighboring granulosa cells as substrates for estrogen synthesis.
*Granulosa Progesterone Production (Direct Action):* Stimulates granulosa cells to produce progesterone.
*Final Follicular Growth (Direct Action):* Acts synergistically with FSH during the final days before ovulation to cause rapid swelling and expansion of the mature Graafian follicle.
*Ovulation Trigger (Direct Action):* The pre-ovulatory LH surge triggers the rupture of the follicular wall (stigma) and release of the oocyte (ovulation).

*Enzyme & Eicosanoid Induction (Direct Action):* Increases proteolytic enzyme activity (e.g. plasminogen activator) and stimulates endoperoxide synthase to increase synthesis of prostaglandins and leukotrienes, driving follicular rupture.

*Luteinization (Direct Action):* Transforms the remaining granulosa and theca interna cells of the ruptured follicle into progesterone-secreting granulosa-lutein and theca-lutein cells, forming the corpus luteum.

*Corpus Luteum Maintenance & Secretion (Direct Action):* Maintains the corpus luteum and promotes its continuous secretion of large amounts of progesterone, estrogen, and androgens during the luteal phase (persisting for ~12 days unless rescued by hCG in pregnancy).
**Male Reproductive System (Testicular Steroidogenesis):**
*Leydig Cell Testosterone Synthesis (Direct Action):* Stimulates Leydig (interstitial) cells of the testes to synthesize and secrete testosterone.
Regulation
**Hypothalamic Axis:** Driven by pulsatile bursts of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) from the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
**Feedback Loops:**
*Negative Feedback (Default):* Low-to-moderate sustained levels of estrogen, progesterone, and androgens inhibit LH secretion via negative feedback at the anterior pituitary and hypothalamus.

*Positive Feedback (Pre-ovulatory Surge):* High sustained levels of estrogen (~200 pg/ml for ~36 hours) during the late follicular phase exert positive feedback on both the hypothalamus (increasing GnRH burst frequency) and anterior pituitary (increasing gonadotrope sensitivity), triggering the pre-ovulatory LH surge.
*Inhibin Feedback:* Inhibin secreted by corpus luteum / Sertoli cells contributes to LH suppression.
Factors Affecting

**Factors Increasing Secretion:** High sustained pre-ovulatory estrogen levels, GnRH bursts, and menopause/climacteric (loss of ovarian negative feedback causes marked elevation in circhoral LH spikes).

**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Continuous (non-pulsatile) GnRH exposure (down-regulates gonadotrope receptors), estrogen/progesterone combination therapy (e.g. oral contraceptives), elevated prolactin, pre-pubertal state, and age-related ovarian failure.
Clinical Correlates
**Hot Flushes:** In menopausal women, hot flushes coincide with episodic circhoral surges of LH.
**LH Resistance:** Decreased number or sensitivity of LH receptors on granulosa/theca cells causes follicular dysfunction and infertility.
**Therapeutic Uses:** Continuous long-acting GnRH analogs are used to treat precocious puberty and prostate cancer by down-regulating gonadotrope LH receptors and suppressing LH and sex steroids.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide.
**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 198 amino acids with a molecular weight of 23,000. Displays considerable structural similarity to human Growth Hormone (GH).
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Anterior pituitary gland.

**Specific Cell Type:** Lactotrophs (constitute 10–25% of anterior pituitary cells; population expands during pregnancy, lactation, and estrogen therapy). Also synthesized by immunocytes (macrophages, NK cells, T cells, B cells).
Synthesis
**Processing:** Synthesized as preproprolactin -> proprolactin -> active prolactin, stored in lactotroph secretory granules.
Secretion

**Pattern:** Diurnal variation under dominant baseline tonic inhibition by dopamine. During pregnancy, plasma levels rise steadily from week 5 to term (10–20 times non-pregnant levels). During lactation, episodic secretory bursts occur during each nursing period (lasting ~1 hour).
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Transmembrane prolactin receptors (homologous to GH receptors in their extracellular domain) on target cell membranes (e.g., lobular alveolar cells of mammary glands).
**Signaling Pathway:** Activates the intracellular JAK-STAT (Janus kinase - Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription) pathway, inducing specific gene transcription.
Target Tissues
Mammary glands (ducts and alveoli), hypothalamus, gonads (ovaries, testes), liver, and immunocytes.
Functions
**Mammary System & Lactation:**
*Glandular Hyperplasia (Direct Action):* Causes hyperplasia of breast tissue before/after puberty, during pregnancy, and during lactation.
*Ductal Development (Permissive/Synergistic Action):* Acts together with estrogen, progesterone, cortisol, and GH to stimulate branching and proliferation of female mammary ducts.
*Lobule-Alveolar Growth (Permissive/Synergistic Action):* Acts along with estrogen and progesterone during pregnancy to increase the lobules of alveoli in the mammary gland.

*Milk Synthesis & Secretion (Direct Action via JAK-STAT):* Stimulates transcription and translation of casein, lactose, and lipid-synthesizing enzymes, driving milk production and secretion in alveolar lobular cells during lactation (acting with insulin and cortisol).
**Reproductive & Behavioral Systems:**

*Lactational Amenorrhea (Indirect Action):* High prolactin levels inhibit hypothalamic GnRH secretion, reducing LH and FSH release to prevent ovulation and cause amenorrhea in lactating mothers (physiological contraception).
*Libido Inhibition (Direct Central Action):* Inhibits sexual libido in both females and males.
*Maternal Behavior (Direct Central Action):* Stimulates maternal affection, bonding, and protective behavior toward newborns.
*Inhibition of Male Spermatogenesis (Direct Action):* Decreases spermatogenesis in male testes.
**Immune System:**
*Immunologic Tolerance of Fetus (Direct Action):* Secreted by maternal immunocytes during pregnancy to promote immunologic balance required for acceptance of fetal tissue.
*Autoreactive B Cell Preservation (Direct Action):* Inhibits the negative selection of autoreactive B lymphocytes.
**Growth & Metabolic System:**

*Synlactin Synthesis (Direct Action on Liver):* Increases hepatic synthesis and secretion of synlactin (an intermediary growth factor structurally analogous to somatomedin), indirectly stimulating growth.
Regulation
**Tonal Inhibition:** Hypothalamic Dopamine (PIF) continuously inhibits prolactin secretion via D2 receptors. Somatostatin and GABA also inhibit release.
**Stimulatory Factors:** Hypothalamic Prolactin-Releasing Factor (PRF), TRH, Oxytocin, Angiotensin II, Serotonin, and Opioids promote release.
**Short-Loop Negative Feedback:** Elevated prolactin stimulates hypothalamic secretion of dopamine and somatostatin, which inhibit further prolactin release.
Factors Affecting

**Factors Increasing Secretion:** Pregnancy, nursing/suckling (nipple receptor stimulation inhibits dopamine release, triggering prolactin pulses), estrogen therapy (causes lactotroph hyperplasia and increases responsiveness), sleep, physical/psychological stress, TRH, dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, reserpine, alpha-methyldopa), serotonin, and opioids.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Dopamine and dopamine agonists (bromocriptine, cabergoline), somatostatin, GABA, prolactin self-feedback, and cessation of nursing.
Clinical Correlates

**Amenorrhea-Galactorrhea Syndrome / Hyperprolactinemia:** Caused by lactotroph tumors (prolactinomas), hypothalamic/pituitary lesions, or drugs (reserpine, phenothiazines, tricyclics). Features: galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility, and loss of libido. Treated with dopaminergic drugs (e.g. bromocriptine) which inhibit prolactin secretion, restoring fertility and libido.
**Deficient Lactation:** Caused by poor breast development, chronic illness, or hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction.
**Chiari-Frommel Syndrome:** Persistent post-partum lactation, amenorrhea, and uterine super-involution due to persistent prolactin without FSH/LH.
Characteristics
**beta-Lipotropin (beta-LPH):** Peptide cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC).
**alpha-MSH:** Peptide consisting of 13 amino acids corresponding to the N-terminal 1–13 sequence of ACTH.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Anterior pituitary corticotrophs (and intermediate lobe/melanocytes where present).
Synthesis

**Precursor & Processing:** Both are derived from the preprohormone precursor **Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)**. Tissue-specific cleavage of POMC by prohormone convertase 1 (PC1) and PC2 yields ACTH, beta-LPH, gamma-LPH, beta-endorphin, alpha-MSH, gamma-MSH, and CLIP. alpha-MSH is formed by cleavage of ACTH.
Secretion
Co-secreted along with ACTH in response to CRH stimulation. Secretion is low under normal conditions but increases significantly whenever the rate of ACTH secretion is high (e.g. Addison's disease).
Target Tissues
Skin melanocytes (located between dermis and epidermis).
Central nervous system (hypothalamus).
Functions
**Integumentary System (alpha-MSH / intrinsic ACTH activity):**
*Melanin Synthesis & Dispersion (Direct Action):* Stimulates the growth and enzymatic activity of skin melanocytes, increasing melanin pigment synthesis and dispersing it into epidermal cells.
**Central Nervous System / Appetite Regulation (alpha-MSH):**
*Anorexigenic Action (Direct Central Action):* Acts on hypothalamic neural circuits to decrease appetite and inhibit food intake.
Regulation
Governed by hypothalamic Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH) which stimulates POMC gene expression and processing, and negative feedback by circulating Cortisol.
Clinical Correlates

**Skin Hyperpigmentation:** Conditions with elevated ACTH/POMC secretion (Addison's disease due to loss of cortisol feedback, or ACTH-secreting pituitary tumors) produce skin hyperpigmentation ("appearing black") due to intrinsic alpha-MSH activity.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Oligopeptide.
**Size/Structure:** Composed of 9 amino acids (Cys-Tyr-Phe-Gln-Asn-Cys-Pro-Arg-Gly-NH2) with an intramolecular disulfide bridge between cysteine residues.
Source

**Gland/Organ:** Synthesized primarily in the magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic nuclei (SO) (~5/6th) and paraventricular nuclei (PVN) (~1/6th) of the hypothalamus. Transported down the hypothalamo-hypophysial tract to be stored in and released from the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).
Synthesis
**Precursor Molecule:** Synthesized as part of the preprohormone precursor **prepro-pressophysin**, which is cleaved into ADH and its carrier protein **neurophysin II** during axonal transport.
Secretion
**Mechanism:** Exocytosis from posterior pituitary nerve endings into capillaries upon action potential propagation.
**Stimuli for Release:**

*Osmotic Stimuli:* Increased plasma osmolality sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors (located in the anterior hypothalamus / AV3V region, organum vasculosum of lamina terminalis [OVLT], and subfornical organ [SFO]). Sensitive to changes as small as 1% in osmolality.

*Hemodynamic Stimuli:* Decreased ECF volume or decreased blood pressure sensed by carotid/aortic baroreceptors and low-pressure atrial stretch receptors (vagal afferents). Requires a ~10% drop in blood volume to trigger, but produces exponential plasma ADH surges up to 100-fold.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**V2 Receptors:** Located on the basolateral membrane of principal cells in renal late distal convoluted tubules (DCT) and collecting ducts.

*Signaling Pathway:* Couples to Gs -> activates adenylyl cyclase -> increases intracellular cAMP -> activates Protein Kinase A -> triggers exocytosis and insertion of **Aquaporin-2 (AQP2)** water channel vesicles into the apical luminal membrane.
**V1A Receptors:** Located on vascular smooth muscle cells.
*Signaling Pathway:* Couples to Gq -> activates Phospholipase C -> generates IP3/DAG -> increases intracellular Ca2+, causing smooth muscle contraction.
**V1B (V3) Receptors:** Located on anterior pituitary corticotrophs.
*Signaling Pathway:* Stimulates synthesis and release of CRH and ACTH.
Target Tissues
Kidneys (DCT, collecting ducts), vascular smooth muscle, brain/spinal cord, anterior pituitary corticotrophs, spermatic cord smooth muscle, and liver.
Functions
**Renal & Fluid Homeostasis System:**

*Renal Water Reabsorption (Direct Action via V2 Receptors):* Increases water permeability of late DCT and collecting ducts by inserting Aquaporin-2 channels, driving passive water reabsorption into the hypertonic medullary interstitium to produce concentrated urine and restore ECF volume/osmolality.
**Cardiovascular & Hemodynamic System:**

*Arteriolar Vasoconstriction (Direct Action via V1A Receptors at Supraphysiological Doses):* Causes potent systemic vasoconstriction of small arterioles to increase total peripheral resistance and elevate arterial blood pressure during severe hypovolemia or acute hemorrhage.
*Cardiac Output Reduction (Direct Action via Area Postrema):* Acts on the area postrema to decrease cardiac output.
**Central Nervous & Behavioral System:**
*Memory Facilitation (Direct Action as Neurotransmitter):* Functions as a neurotransmitter in memory areas of the brain to facilitate memory retention and learning.
**Endocrine System:**
*Potentiation of HPA Axis (Direct Action via V1B Receptors):* Stimulates hypothalamic CRH release and directly acts on pituitary corticotrophs to increase ACTH secretion.
**Reproductive & Metabolic Systems:**
*Spermatic Muscle Contraction & Ejaculation (Direct Action via V1 Receptors):* Contracts smooth muscle of the spermatic cord and vas deferens to facilitate sperm ejaculation.
*Hepatic Glycogenolysis (Direct Action):* Stimulates glycogen breakdown in the liver.
Regulation
**Feedback Loop:** Water reabsorption dilutes plasma solutes, restoring ECF osmolality to normal and shutting off osmoreceptor discharge.
**Atrial Volume Reflex / ANP:** Increased atrial fill/stretch inhibits ADH release and stimulates ANP, promoting diuresis.
Factors Affecting

**Factors Increasing Secretion:** Increased plasma osmolality, decreased ECF volume / hypovolemia, hypotension, Angiotensin II, nausea and vomiting (up to 100-fold surge), physical pain, emotion, hypoglycemia, standing, heat, nicotine, morphine, and hypoxia.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Decreased plasma osmolality, increased ECF volume / hypervolemia, ANP, alcohol / ethanol, cold temperature, cortisol, thyroxine, and alpha-adrenergic agonists.
Metabolism and Clearance
Rapidly inactivated in the liver and kidneys; biological half-life is approximately 18 minutes.
Clinical Correlates

**Diabetes Insipidus (DI):** ADH deficiency (central DI) or renal unresponsiveness (nephrogenic DI) characterized by excretion of large volumes of dilute urine (polyuria) and secondary thirst (polydipsia).
**Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH (SIADH):** Unregulated high ADH secretion (from lung cancers, brain diseases) causing water retention, hyponatremia, and cerebral/pulmonary salt wasting.
**Vasopressin Escape:** Down-regulation of aquaporin-2 expression in collecting ducts during chronic SIADH/tumors to limit severe hyponatremia.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Oligopeptide.
**Size/Structure:** Composed of 9 amino acids (differing from ADH by 2 amino acids).
Source

**Gland/Organ:** Synthesized mainly in the magnocellular neurons of the paraventricular nuclei (PVN) (~5/6th) and supraoptic nuclei (SO) (~1/6th) of the hypothalamus. Stored in and secreted from the posterior pituitary gland. Also present in the ovary.
Synthesis
**Precursor Molecule:** Synthesized as part of the preprohormone precursor **prepro-oxyphysin**, which includes oxytocin, **neurophysin I**, and a glycoprotein.
Secretion
**Mechanism:** Secreted via exocytosis from posterior pituitary nerve endings into capillaries upon neural reflex arc activation.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptors:** Transmembrane G-protein coupled oxytocin receptors on uterine myometrium, mammary myoepithelial cells, ovarian corpus luteum, and male vas deferens.
Target Tissues
Female breasts (myoepithelial cells surrounding alveoli), uterus (myometrium), ovaries (corpus luteum), male genital tract (vas deferens smooth muscle), and cardiovascular/pancreatic tissue.
Functions
**Mammary System & Lactation:**

*Milk Ejection / Let-Down Reflex (Direct Action):* Contracts myoepithelial cells surrounding the milk-laden alveoli of the mammary glands, forcing milk from alveoli into mammary ducts and out through the nipple (neurohumoral reflex responding to suckling in < 1 minute).
**Female Reproductive System & Parturition:**

*Parturition / Labor Contractions (Direct Action):* Stimulates vigorous rhythmic contractions of the myometrium during labor to initiate and complete birth (neurohumoral positive-feedback reflex driven by fetal head pressing on the cervix).
*Uterine Sperm Transport (Direct Action):* Causes post-coital contractions of the non-pregnant uterus to facilitate passive transport of deposited sperm up into the fallopian tubes.
*Luteolysis Support (Direct Local Action):* Present in ovaries where it acts locally as a luteolysin to facilitate degeneration of the corpus luteum at the end of an unfertilized menstrual cycle.
**Male Reproductive System:**
*Sperm Propulsion (Direct Action):* Increases during male orgasm/ejaculation, contracting smooth muscle of the vas deferens to propel sperm toward the urethra.
**Behavioral & Central Nervous System:**
*Maternal Attachment & Bonding (Direct Central Action):* Elevated during pregnancy/postpartum to promote maternal attachment, infant-directed gaze, affectionate touch, caregiving, and social bonding.
**Cardiovascular & Metabolic Systems:**
*Glucose Homeostasis:* Increases insulin secretion and enhances insulin sensitivity.
*Blood Pressure Modulation:* Decreases blood pressure by modulating central autonomic regulation.
Regulation

**Milk Ejection Reflex (Neurohumoral Arc):** Nipple suckling -> sensory nerves -> spinothalamic collaterals -> PVN/SO cholinergic stimulation -> posterior pituitary oxytocin surge -> myoepithelial contraction.

**Parturition Reflex (Positive Feedback Loop):** Cervical stretch -> spinal sensory afferents -> hypothalamic PVN stimulation -> oxytocin release -> increased myometrial contraction -> further cervical stretch.
Factors Affecting

**Factors Increasing Secretion:** Nipple suckling, cervical dilatation/distension during labor, female genital stimulation during coitus, emotional/psychological stress, and increasing estrogen-to-progesterone ratio toward term (up-regulates uterine oxytocin receptors).
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Alcohol / ethanol (inhibits oxytocin release).
Clinical Correlates

**Oxytocic Therapy (Exogenous Oxytocin):** Used routinely in clinical obstetrics for (1) induction of labor when pain is inadequate at term, (2) acceleration of labor progress, and (3) immediate post-placental administration to prevent postpartum hemorrhage.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Amine / Amino acid derivatives (iodinated tyronines).
**Thyroxine (T4):** Contains 4 iodine atoms (3,5,3',5'-tetraiodothyronine); accounts for ~93% of total thyroid gland output. Functions primarily as a circulating prohormone.
**Triiodothyronine (T3):** Contains 3 iodine atoms (3,5,3'-triiodothyronine); accounts for ~7% of direct thyroid output. Possesses 4 times higher rapid biological activity/potency than T4.
**Reverse T3 (rT3):** Physiologically inactive/inert isomer (3,5',3'-triiodothyronine).
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Thyroid gland (follicular epithelial cells / thyrocytes surrounding colloid-filled follicles).
Synthesis
**Substrates:** Iodide (I-) absorbed from diet and Tyrosine residues within Thyroglobulin (glycoprotein, MW 660,000, containing 123 tyrosine residues).
**Key Steps & Enzymes:**

*Iodide Trapping:* Active secondary cotransport of I- across the basolateral membrane via the Na+-I- Symporter (NIS), accumulating I- 20–40 times plasma concentration (TSH upregulates NIS). Iodine is actively transported across the apical membrane into colloid by Pendrin (CN–I- anion exchanger).

*Oxidation & Organification:* Iodide is oxidized to reactive iodine by **Thyroid Peroxidase (TPO)** and attached to 3-position of tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin to form Monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and Diiodotyrosine (DIT).
*Coupling Reaction:* Facilitated by Thyroid Peroxidase (TPO). Condensation of DIT + DIT forms Thyroxine (T4); condensation of MIT + DIT forms Triiodothyronine (T3); DIT + MIT forms rT3.
*Storage:* Hormones remain stored bound to thyroglobulin inside colloid for weeks/months.
*Proteolysis & Secretion:* Endocytosis of colloid droplets into thyrocytes -> lysosomal fusion -> proteolysis of thyroglobulin -> free T4 and T3 diffuse across basolateral membrane into blood.
Transport
**Protein Bound Fraction:** Over 99% of circulating T4 and T3 is bound to plasma proteins synthesized by the liver.
*Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG):* Binds the majority of T4 and T3 with high affinity.
*Transthyretin / Thyroxine-Binding Prealbumin (TBPA):* Binds T4.
*Albumin:* Binds 55% of T3 and 10% of T4 with lower affinity.
**Free Fraction:** Less than 1% exists in free active equilibrium, which provides feedback and enters target cells.
**Half-Life:** T4 half-life = **7 days** (high affinity binding); T3 half-life = **1 day**.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action

**Intracellular / Nuclear Receptors:** T3 and T4 enter cells via carrier-mediated energy-dependent transport. Inside the cell, T4 is deiodinated to T3. T3 enters the nucleus to bind Thyroid Hormone Receptors (TRalpha1, TRbeta1, TRbeta2) attached as heterodimers with Retinoid X Receptor (RXR) to Thyroid Response Elements (TRE) on DNA.
**Downstream Actions:** Drives gene transcription and mRNA translation into hundreds of new intracellular enzymes, structural proteins, respiratory enzymes, and Na+-K+ ATPase pumps.
Target Tissues
Virtually all tissues and organs in the body (except adult brain and gonads which are less metabolic-sensitive).
Functions
**Basal Metabolic Rate & Thermogenesis:**

*Oxygen Consumption & Heat Production (Direct Action via Na+-K+ ATPase & Mitochondria):* Increases Na+-K+ ATPase activity, mitochondrial size/number, and respiratory enzyme synthesis, markedly increasing cellular oxygen consumption, Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR), and heat production throughout the body.
*Thermogenin Expression (Direct Action on Brown Fat):* T3 stimulates production of thermogenin (UCP-1) in brown adipose tissue to mediate catecholamine-induced non-shivering thermogenesis.
**Cardiovascular System:**
*Cardiac Output & Stroke Volume (Direct & Permissive Actions):* Increases cardiac output, heart rate, myocardial contractility, and stroke volume.
*Myosin ATPase Activity (Direct Action):* Increases myosin ATPase activity, enhancing excitation-contraction coupling in cardiac myocytes.
*Beta-Adrenergic Receptor Upregulation (Permissive Action):* Increases expression and sensitivity of beta1-adrenergic receptors to catecholamines in nodal tissues and ventricular muscle.
*Myocardial Hypertrophy (Direct Action):* Stimulates protein synthesis in cardiac myocytes, inducing physiological ventricular hypertrophy.
**Metabolic & Intermediary Systems:**
*Carbohydrate Metabolism (Direct Action):* Enhances intestinal glucose absorption, stimulates gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and cellular glucose uptake.
*Lipid Metabolism (Direct Action):* Accelerates lipolysis (releasing free fatty acids and glycerol), increases lipid turnover and beta-oxidation.

*Cholesterol Clearance (Direct Action):* Increases hepatic expression of LDL receptors, promoting cholesterol uptake, oxidation, and biliary excretion, thereby significantly reducing plasma cholesterol and total lipids.
*Protein Turnover (Direct Action):* Promotes muscle proteolysis and overall protein turnover/degradation.
**Central Nervous System & Development:**

*Fetal/Infant Brain Maturation (Direct Action during Development):* Essential for fetal/infant neuronal sprouting, myelination, and dendritic arborization (deficiency causes permanent cretinism/mental retardation).
**Growth & Skeletal System:**
*Somatic Growth (Permissive/Direct Action):* Synergizes with Growth Hormone and IGF-1 to promote linear bone growth, skeletal maturation, and epiphyseal ossification.
Types / Isoforms
**Thyroxine (T4):** Main prohormone secreted.
**Triiodothyronine (T3):** Primary active intracellular hormone.
**Reverse T3 (rT3):** Inactive metabolite.
**Tetraiodoacetic Acid (Tetrac):** Minor metabolite.
Regulation
**Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Thyroid (HPT) Axis:** Hypothalamic TRH -> Pituitary TSH -> Thyroid T4/T3.
**Negative Feedback Loop:** Free T3 and T4 exert negative feedback on pituitary thyrotrophs (inhibiting TSH) and hypothalamic PVN (inhibiting TRH).
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion:** TSH, cold exposure (via TRH), and high iodine supply (within physiological range).
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Iodine deficiency (causes goiter/hypothyroidism), Somatostatin, Dopamine, Cortisol, GH, prolonged fasting, and severe illness.
Metabolism and Clearance

**Peripheral Deiodination:** ~35% of secreted T4 is converted to active T3 peripherally by 5'-deiodinase (Type 1 [D1] in liver/kidney and Type 2 [D2] in brain/pituitary). ~45% of T4 is converted to inactive rT3 by Type 3 (D3) 5-deiodinase. T3 is further deiodinated to diiodothyronines.

**Conjugation & Excretion:** ~20% of T4/T3 is conjugated with sulfates and glucuronides in the liver, secreted in bile into the intestine (re-entering enterohepatic circulation); ~4% iodine is excreted in stool and ~480 micrograms/day in urine.
Clinical Correlates
**Cretinism (Infant Hypothyroidism):** Congenital thyroid deficiency resulting in severe mental retardation, short stature/dwarfism, and delayed skeletal development.
**Myxedema (Adult Hypothyroidism):** Features: low BMR, cold intolerance, weight gain, puffiness, lethargy, bradycardia, and high TSH.

**Hyperthyroidism / Graves' Disease:** Features: high BMR, heat intolerance, weight loss, nervousness, tachycardia, excessive sweating, hyper-sympathetic state (alleviated by beta-blockers like propranolol), and low/undetectable TSH.
Name with Synonyms
Calcitonin, Thyrocalcitonin.
Characteristics
Peptide / polypeptide hormone composed of 32 amino acids with a molecular weight of approximately 3,400 to 3,500.
Properties
Normal plasma concentration is 10–20 pg/mL (increases up to 10-fold in hypercalcemia). Biological half-life is short, lasting 5–10 minutes.
Source

Secreted by parafollicular cells (C cells) located in the interstitial fluid between thyroid follicles (constituting ~0.1% of the human thyroid gland). C cells develop from the ultimobranchial bodies derived from the 5th branchial pouch.
Synthesis
Transcribed from the calcitonin gene in thyroid C cells. (Alternative tissue-specific splicing of the same gene mRNA in the nervous system forms Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide [CGRP]).
Secretion
Primary stimulus is a rise in plasma calcium concentration above 9 mg/dL (or a 10% increase above normal ECF calcium, inducing an immediate 2-fold or greater surge in secretion).
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
*Receptor Type & Location:* Calcitonin GPCRs located on target cell membranes (osteoclasts, renal tubule cells).
*Signaling Pathway & Second Messenger:* Coupled to Gs proteins, activating the adenylyl cyclase–cyclic AMP (cAMP) system.
Target Tissues
Bone (osteoclasts) and Kidneys (renal tubular cells).
Functions
*Skeletal System / Bone (Direct Actions):*
Rapidly decreases the resorptive activity of osteoclasts and osteocytic membranes (immediate effect within minutes).
Reduces the formation, differentiation, size, and total number of new osteoclasts (prolonged effect).
Inhibits bone resorption, decreasing calcium release/turnover into plasma.
Decreases plasma phosphate levels by inhibiting bone resorption and facilitating phosphate entry into bone matrix (independent of its hypocalcemic effect).
Protects maternal bone against excessive resorption during pregnancy and lactation (counteracts 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol-induced bone loss).
Protects against postprandial hypercalcemia following food intake.
*Renal System (Direct Actions):*
Decreases tubular reabsorption of calcium, producing calciuria.
Decreases tubular reabsorption of phosphate in proximal tubules, producing mild phosphaturia.
*Central Nervous System (Direct Action as Co-transmitter):*
Co-localized with CGRP in brain regions (pituitary, hypothalamus, limbic system) to inhibit central pain impulse transmission (opioid-independent central analgesia).
Types / Related Molecules
Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP; potent vasodilator formed in the nervous system).
Regulation
Regulated by plasma calcium levels via a weak negative feedback loop that operates opposite to the PTH system.
Factors Affecting

*Increases Secretion:* Elevated plasma calcium (>9 mg/dL), beta-adrenergic receptor agonists, dopamine, gastrointestinal hormones (gastrin—a potent stimulus, CCK, glucagon, secretin), feeding, and estrogen.
Metabolism and Clearance
Rapidly degraded in the liver. Biological half-life is 5–10 minutes.
Clinical Correlates

*Calcitonin Escape Phenomenon:* The hypocalcemic/anti-resorptive effect wanes within hours due to rapid down-regulation of calcitonin receptors, limiting its long-term efficacy in managing hypercalcemia.
*Medullary Carcinoma of the Thyroid:* C-cell tumor causing hypersecretion of calcitonin; bone structure remains essentially normal due to the calcitonin escape phenomenon.
*Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome & Pernicious Anemia:* High circulating gastrin levels cause secondary hypersecretion of calcitonin.
*Therapeutic Uses:* Used clinically in acute hypercalcemia, Paget's disease (to suppress localized osteoclastic activity), and as a central analgesic.
Name with Synonyms
Parathyroid Hormone, PTH, Parathormone.
Characteristics
Polypeptide containing 84 amino acids with a molecular weight of approximately 9,500. Biological calcium-regulating activity resides in the N-terminal 1–34 (or 1–27) amino acid sequence.
Properties
Normal plasma concentration is 10–60 pg/mL. Biological half-life is approximately 10 minutes.
Source

Parathyroid glands (normally 4 glands located behind the upper and lower poles of the thyroid gland). Secreted by chief cells (predominant functional parenchymal cells with prominent Golgi apparatus and secretory vesicles). Oxyphil cells do not normally secrete PTH.
Synthesis
Synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum as a 115-amino acid precursor called **prepro-PTH**.
A 25-amino acid leader sequence is cleaved in the ER to form **pro-PTH** (90 amino acids).
In the Golgi apparatus, another 6 amino acids are removed from the N-terminal to form active **PTH** (84 amino acids).
Packaged and stored in secretory granules of chief cells.
Secretion
Primary stimulus is a decrease in ECF ionized calcium concentration. Monitored by Calcium-Sensing Receptors (CaSR) on chief cell membranes.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
*Receptors:* Type 1 (PTH 1R; binds PTH and PTHrP, present in bone and kidney), Type 2 (PTH 2R; binds PTH only, present in brain, pancreas, placenta), and Type 3 (CPTH; reacts with C-terminal).
