Binds to **LH receptors** on target cell membranes (e.g., corpus luteum, fetal Leydig cells), activating the adenylyl cyclase–cAMP second messenger system.
Target Tissues
Ovarian corpus luteum, fetal Leydig cells (interstitial cells), maternal brain (vomiting center), maternal thyroid, and placenta.
Functions
**Corpus Luteum & Pregnancy Maintenance (Primary Action):**
*Luteotropic / Rescue Action:* Prevents involution of the corpus luteum at the end of the monthly female sexual cycle, rescuing it to form the corpus luteum of pregnancy.

*Hyperplasia & Steroidogenesis:* Stimulates the corpus luteum to grow to twice its initial size and secrete massive quantities of progesterone, estrogens, and inhibin, maintaining the decidualized endometrium and preventing menstruation/spontaneous abortion.
**Male Fetal Differentiation:**

*Interstitial Cell Stimulation:* Exerts an LH-like trophic effect on the Leydig cells of male fetuses, stimulating them to produce testosterone necessary for Wolffian duct differentiation and male external genitalia formation.
*Testicular Descent:* Stimulates fetal testosterone output near term to drive testicular descent into the scrotum.
**Central Nervous System:**
*Emesis Stimulation:* Stimulates vomiting centers in the brain, producing **morning sickness** (nausea and vomiting) during the first trimester.
**Maternal Endocrine Modulation:**

*Thyroid Stimulation:* Exerts a weak thyrotropic effect on the maternal thyroid gland (alongside human chorionic thyrotropin), contributing to maternal thyroid enlargement and increased thyroxine output.
*Relaxin Stimulation:* Drives secretion of relaxin from the corpus luteum and placenta.
Clinical Correlates
*Pregnancy Diagnostic Tests:* Radioimmunoassay (RIA) detection of hCG in plasma (6 days post-conception) or urine tests (14 days post-conception) forms the basis of early pregnancy diagnosis.
*Ovulation Induction:* Administered therapeutically as an LH analog to trigger ovulation in infertile women with pituitary gonadotropin deficiency.
*Tumor Marker:* Secreted by chorionic tumors (hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma) and certain gastrointestinal malignancies.

hormones.name: Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS / Human Placental Lactogen - hPL / Chorionic Growth Hormone)

blocks.tx: Characteristics

Protein / polypeptide hormone containing 191 amino acids with a molecular weight of 22,000. Shares structural homology with human Growth Hormone (GH) and Prolactin (PRL), derived from a common gene precursor.
Properties
Secreted in massive quantities—greater in weight than all other placental hormones combined.
Source
Secreted by **syncytiotrophoblast cells** of the placenta.
Secretion
Begins around the 3rd to 5th week of pregnancy. Secretion rises progressively throughout gestation in direct proportion to placental weight, reaching a peak plasma concentration of ~15 mg/mL at term.
Target Tissues
Maternal mammary glands, maternal adipose tissue, maternal skeletal muscle, and fetal tissues.
Functions
**Mammary System & Lactogenesis:** Promotes growth and structural development of maternal mammary glands and displays weak lactogenic activity (preparing breasts for lactation alongside prolactin).
**Fetal Somatic Growth:** Directly stimulates somatic tissue growth and protein deposition in the fetus, acting as the "growth hormone of pregnancy".
**Maternal & Fetal Fuel Metabolism:**

*Maternal Lipolysis:* Stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase in maternal adipose tissue, releasing large amounts of free fatty acids (FFAs) into maternal blood to provide an alternative energy source for maternal tissues.
*Maternal Diabetogenic Action (Anti-Insulin):* Decreases insulin sensitivity and glucose utilization in the mother, inducing maternal glucose intolerance.

*Fetal Nutrient Availability:* By shunting maternal metabolism toward FFA consumption and creating mild maternal hyperglycemia, it ensures a continuous, abundant supply of glucose and amino acids across the placenta to the growing fetus.
Clinical Correlates
*Placental Function Test:* Plasma hCS concentration is directly proportional to total placental mass; low hCS levels in the third trimester serve as a diagnostic indicator of placental insufficiency.
A. Placental Estrogens (Estriol, 17-β-Estradiol, Estrone)
Characteristics
Steroid hormones (C-18 steroids). The major estrogen produced by the placenta is **Estriol (E₃)** (secreted in very low amounts in non-pregnant females).
Source & Fetoplacental Unit Synthesis
Secreted by the **syncytiotrophoblast cells** of the placenta.
*Fetoplacental Unit Requirement:* The placenta lacks the enzyme *17,20-lyase* and *16α-hydroxylase*, and cannot synthesize estrogens *de novo* from basic acetate or cholesterol substrates.

*Synthesis Pipeline:* Maternal and fetal adrenals synthesize Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS). Fetal liver/adrenal *16α-hydroxylase* converts DHEAS to 16-OH-DHEAS. The placenta takes up DHEAS and 16-OH-DHEAS, removes sulfate via placental sulfatase, and uses placental **aromatase** to convert DHEA into **17-β-Estradiol** and 16-OH-DHEA into **Estriol (E₃)**.
Secretion
Secretion increases progressively during the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, reaching a peak at term (up to 30 times normal non-pregnant levels).
Target Tissues
Maternal uterus (endometrium, myometrium, cervix), breasts, pelvic joints/ligaments, external genitalia, and fetal tissues.
Functions

**Uterine & Cervical Growth & Sensitization:** Causes marked hypertrophy and enlargement of the pregnant uterus; increases myometrial smooth muscle contractile protein content, excitability, and gap junction (connexin) formation; upregulates myometrial **oxytocin receptors** in late pregnancy; and promotes enzymatic lysis of cervical collagen fibers to soften the cervix.
**Mammary Ductal System:** Stimulates growth, elongation, and branching of maternal breast ductal networks and fat deposition in breast stroma.
**Pelvic Ligaments:** Relaxes maternal pelvic ligaments, limbering sacroiliac joints and making the symphysis pubis elastic to facilitate fetal passage through the birth canal during labor.

**Maternal Cardiovascular & Fluid Balance:** Upregulates hepatic synthesis of Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG); promotes renal tubular sodium and water reabsorption (contributing to plasma volume expansion).
**Fetal Growth:** Influences early embryonic cell division rates and organogenesis.
Clinical Correlates

*Fetal Well-Being Marker:* Because estriol synthesis depends directly on fetal adrenal/liver 16-OH-DHEA precursor output, maternal 24-hour urinary or plasma **estriol (E₃) levels** serve as a direct clinical index of fetal health and fetoplacental integrity.
B. Placental Progesterone
Characteristics
Steroid hormone (C-21 progestin).
Source & Fetoplacental Unit Synthesis
Secreted by the **syncytiotrophoblast cells** of the placenta.

*Synthesis Pipeline:* The placenta cannot synthesize cholesterol *de novo* from acetate, but takes up maternal LDL cholesterol from blood, converting it via *cholesterol desmolase* and *3β-HSD* to pregnenolone and then **progesterone**.

Placental progesterone diffuses into maternal blood to exert systemic actions and into fetal blood where it serves as the essential substrate for fetal adrenal synthesis of **cortisol**, corticosterone, and androgens.
Secretion

Placental production begins around week 6–8 of gestation and fully replaces corpus luteum function by the 7th–12th week. Secretion increases exponentially to reach tremendous levels (~250–300 mg/day) in late pregnancy.
Target Tissues
Maternal uterine endometrium/myometrium, fallopian tubes, breasts, immune system, and fetal adrenals.
Functions
**Endometrium & Decidualization:** Converts endometrial stromal cells into glycogen- and lipid-rich **decidual cells** that nourish the early blastocyst before full placental formation.

**Myometrial Quiescence (Anti-Abortive Action):** Maintains pregnancy by decreasing myometrial resting membrane potential, suppressing spontaneous electrical spikes, decreasing uterine sensitivity to oxytocin, and opposing prostaglandin actions—preventing premature uterine contractions and spontaneous abortion.
**Fallopian Tube & Uterine Secretions:** Increases mucosal glandular secretions ("uterine milk") to nourish the pre-implantation morula and blastocyst.

**Mammary Lobuloalveolar Development:** Acts synergistically with estrogen, prolactin, and hCS to promote development, budding, and structural enlargement of breast lobules and alveoli (while suppressing actual milk secretion until delivery).
**Substrate for Fetal Corticosteroids:** Provides the precursor molecule for fetal adrenal synthesis of glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids.

**Maternal Respiration & Vasodilation:** Stimulates the medullary respiratory center (increasing minute ventilation and lowering arterialPCO₂) and causes vascular smooth muscle relaxation (lowering diastolic blood pressure).
Clinical Correlates

*Luteal-Placental Shift:* Removal of the corpus luteum before the 7th week of pregnancy causes spontaneous abortion; after the 7th–12th week, placental progesterone production is sufficient to maintain pregnancy independently.
Characteristics
*Chemical Class:* Polypeptide hormone.
*Size / Structure:* Large polypeptide with a molecular weight of approximately 2000. The functional activity of gastrin resides in its C-terminal four amino acids.
Properties
*Half-life:* Short circulating half-life in blood; G-14 and G-17 have a half-life of 2–5 minutes, whereas G-34 has a half-life of about 15 minutes.
Source
*Primary Gland / Organ:* Produced mainly by G cells located in the antral region (pyloric glands) of the stomach and the mucosa of the duodenum.
*Secondary / Extra-gastric Sources:* Also synthesized in the hypothalamus, anterior pituitary, medulla, and fetal pancreas. Functions as a neurotransmitter secreted from the vagus and sciatic nerves.
Synthesis

Synthesized via the regulated peptide pathway: preprohormone (containing a signal peptide) translated in the rough endoplasmic reticulum→ prohormone→ active hormone packaged into secretory granules in the Golgi apparatus.
Secretion

*Stimuli for Release:* Gastric distension (mechanical stretch), products of protein digestion (peptides and amino acids) in the stomach, vagal discharge via Gastrin-Releasing Polypeptide (GRP; non-cholinergic mechanism), epinephrine, and calcium.
*Mechanism:* Exocytosis from G-cell secretory granules into systemic circulation.
Transport
Circulates unbound (free fraction) in general circulation.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
*Receptor Type & Location:* Binds toCCK-B / gastrin receptors located on the cell membranes of parietal cells and enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric mucosa.
*Signaling Pathway & Second Messengers:* Couples to membrane phospholipase C, generating inositol triphosphate (IP₃) and diacylglycerol (DAG) to elevate intracellular free calcium (Ca²⁺).
*Downstream Effects:* Increased cytosolic calcium activates protein kinases that stimulate theH⁺–K⁺ ATPase pump on parietal cell apical membranes, driving active hydrochloric acid (HCl) secretion.
Target Tissues
Stomach (parietal cells, ECL cells, chief cells, gastric smooth muscle), gastro-esophageal junction, duodenum, exocrine and endocrine pancreas, colon, and GI vascular smooth muscle.
Functions
*Gastric System:*
**Direct Action on Parietal Cells:** Acts as the most potent natural stimulator ofHCl secretion from gastric parietal cells.
**Direct Action on ECL Cells:** Stimulates histamine secretion from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells. Histamine then acts locally onH₂ receptors to further drive parietal cellHCl output.
**Direct Action on Chief Cells:** Stimulates pepsinogen and pepsin secretion.
**Direct Trophic Action:** Stimulates hyperplastic growth and structural maintenance of the gastric mucosa and small intestinal mucosa.
**Direct Action on Gastric Motility:** Stimulates gastric smooth muscle motility and enhances pyloric pump propulsive contractions to facilitate stomach emptying.
**Direct Action on Lower Esophageal Sphincter:** Causes contraction of smooth muscle at the gastro-esophageal junction, increasing lower esophageal sphincter tone to prevent reflux esophagitis.
*Intestinal & Colonic Systems:*
**Direct Action on Large Intestine:** Stimulates mass movement and smooth muscle contractions of the colon, mediating the gastrocolic reflex that initiates defecation following a meal.
*Pancreatic System:*
**Direct Action on Exocrine Pancreas:** Stimulates exocrine pancreatic enzyme secretion.
**Direct Action on Endocrine Pancreas:** Stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells.
*Vascular System:*
**Direct Local Action:** Induces mucosal vasodilation, increasing local gastrointestinal blood flow during active digestion.
Types / Isoforms
*G-34 (Big Gastrin):* 34 amino acids.
*G-17 (Little Gastrin):* 17 amino acids; the principal form secreted by the stomach and the primary stimulator of gastric acid secretion.
*G-14 (Mini-Gastrin):* 14 amino acids.
*Other Forms:* C-tetrapeptide (minigastrin) and G-45 (megagastrin).
*Synthetic Analog:* **Pentagastrin** (composed of the terminal 4 amino acids of natural gastrin plus alanine; retains full physiological potency).
Regulation
*Negative Feedback / Autoregulation:* Highly acidic gastric content (pH < 2) directly suppresses G cells and triggers local release of somatostatin, shutting off gastrin release.
*Inhibitory Hormones:* Somatostatin, secretin, GIP, VIP, calcitonin, and glucagon directly inhibit gastrin secretion.
Factors Affecting

*Increases Secretion:* Gastric distension, protein breakdown products, non-cholinergic vagal nerve stimulation (via GRP), epinephrine, calcium, spicy foods/stress ("hurry, worry, curry"), and achlorhydria/pernicious anemia (loss of negative feedback).
*Decreases Secretion:* Intra-gastric acid (pH < 2), somatostatin, secretin, GIP, VIP, calcitonin, and glucagon.
Metabolism and Clearance
Inactivated in the small intestine and degraded in the kidneys.
Clinical Correlates

*Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (Gastrinoma):* Non-α, non-β cell neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreatic islets or duodenum that secretes excessive gastrin. Causes severe, chronic hypergastrinemia, hyperchlorhydria, and refractory peptic ulcer disease. Also increases calcitonin secretion.
*Pernicious Anemia:* Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells leads to achlorhydria, triggering massive compensatory feedback secretion of gastrin from G cells.
*Peptic Ulcer Disease:* Hypergastrinemia drives excessive acid-pepsin output, eroding mucosal defenses.

*Diagnostic Tests:* Fasting serum gastrin estimation by RIA (normal: 20–150 pg/mL); Gastrin provocative tests (Secretin infusion test and Calcium infusion test); Pentagastrin secretory test (evaluates Maximal Acid Output).
Characteristics
*Chemical Class:* Polypeptide hormone.
*Size / Structure:* Molecular weight of approximately 4200. The terminal 5 amino acids are identical to gastrin, and biological activity resides in the C-terminal 8 amino acids.
Properties
*Half-life:* Approximately 5 minutes.
Source
*Primary Source:* Secreted by **I cells** in the mucosa of the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).
*Neural Source:* Functions as a neurotransmitter in the cerebral cortex, somatic nerves, enteric and pancreatic nerves, distal ileum, and colon.
Synthesis
Translated as a preprohormone precursor and cleaved into functional active peptides.
Secretion
*Stimuli for Release:* Contact of intestinal mucosa with protein and fat digestion products—specifically long-chain fatty acids, peptides, amino acids, proteoses, and peptones.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
*Receptor Types & Subtypes:*CCK-A receptors (located peripherally in the gallbladder, pancreas, and GI tract) andCCK-B receptors (located in central brain structures).
*Signaling Pathway & Second Messengers:* Activates membrane phospholipase C to produceIP₃ and DAG, raising intracellular free calcium (Ca²⁺).
*Downstream Effects:* Intracellular calcium surges drive exocytosis of pancreatic digestive enzymes and smooth muscle contraction.
Target Tissues
Gallbladder, exocrine pancreatic acinar cells, stomach, pyloric sphincter, sphincter of Oddi, small intestine, colon, cerebral cortex, and peripheral nerves.
Functions
*Biliary & Gallbladder System:*
**Direct Action on Gallbladder:** Serves as the most potent stimulus driving gallbladder smooth muscle contraction to eject stored bile into the duodenum following a fatty meal.
**Direct Action on Sphincter of Oddi:** Causes relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, allowing bile and pancreatic secretions to flow into the duodenal lumen.
*Pancreatic System:*

**Direct Action on Acinar Cells:** Stimulates exocrine pancreatic secretion exceptionally rich in digestive enzymes (accounting for 70–80% of total postprandial enzyme output; termed pancreozymin / CCK-PZ).
**Synergistic Action:** Augments secretin-driven alkaline fluid and bicarbonate output.
**Trophic Action:** Promotes growth and structural development of the exocrine pancreas.
*Gastric System:*
**Direct Action on Gastric Motility:** Inhibits gastric motility and opposes gastrin-mediated contractions, delaying gastric emptying to prevent duodenal overload (enterogastrone effect).
**Direct Action on Parietal Cells:** Inhibits gastric acid output.
**Direct Action on Pyloric Sphincter:** Augments pyloric sphincter contraction, preventing duodenal-to-gastric reflux.
*Intestinal System:*
**Direct Action on Enterocytes:** Increases synthesis and secretion of enterokinase.
**Direct Action on Intestinal Motility:** Enhances small intestinal peristalsis and stimulates colonic movements to mediate the gastrocolic reflex.
*Endocrine & Metabolic System:*
**Direct Action on Islet Cells:** Stimulates secretion of glucagon and insulin.
*Central Nervous System & Behavior:*
**Anorexigenic Action:** Functions as a central neurotransmitter that suppresses appetite and induces postprandial satiety.
**Emotional / Sensory Actions:** Modulates central perception to induce analgesia and anxiety.
*Vascular System:*
**Direct Action:** Causes local intestinal mucosal vasodilation during active digestion.
Types / Isoforms
*CCK-58, CCK-39, CCK-33, CCK-12, CCK-8, and CCK-4* (carboxyl-terminal tetrapeptide).
Duodenum and jejunum secrete primarily CCK-12 and CCK-8.
Enteric and pancreatic nerves contain mainly CCK-4.
Brain structures express primarily CCK-58 and CCK-8.
Regulation

*Positive Feedback Loop:* Fatty acids and peptides stimulate I cells to release CCK→ CCK increases bile and pancreatic juice output→ enhanced digestion yields more fatty acids and peptides→ further drives CCK release until chyme empties.
Factors Affecting
*Increases:* Fatty acids, long-chain fats, peptides, amino acids, proteoses, peptones, bile, and pancreatic juice.
*Decreases:* Removal of digestive products, somatostatin.
Metabolism and Clearance
Half-life is approximately 5 minutes.
Characteristics
*Chemical Class:* Polypeptide hormone.
*Size / Structure:* Single chain of 27 amino acids with a molecular weight of approximately 3400. All 27 amino acids are essential for biological activity.
*Identifying Feature:* Discovered by Bayliss and Starling in 1902 as the **first hormone** ever identified.
Source
Secreted from **S cells** located in the mucosa of the upper small intestine (duodenum and upper jejunum).
Synthesis
Preprohormone processing in the rough ER and Golgi apparatus into mature 27-amino acid peptide.
Secretion
*Stimuli for Release:* Highly acidic chyme entering the upper intestine (release begins when duodenalpH < 4.5–5.0 and surges atpH < 3.0) and products of protein digestion.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
*Receptor Type & Location:* Cell-membrane GPCRs on pancreatic ductal epithelial cells, cholangiocytes, and gastric mucosa.
*Signaling Pathway & Second Messenger:* Activates membrane adenylyl cyclase, raising intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP).
*Downstream Effects:* cAMP activates protein kinases to stimulate active bicarbonate and fluid transport.
Target Tissues
Pancreatic ductal cells, liver/biliary ductules, gastric parietal cells, G cells, gastric smooth muscle, pyloric sphincter, and pancreatic beta cells.
Functions
*Pancreatic System:*

**Direct Action on Ductal Cells:** Drives copious exocrine pancreatic secretion exceptionally rich in bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ up to 145 mEq/L,pH ~ 8.0) and water, neutralizing acidic duodenal chyme to create an optimal alkaline environment (pH 7.0–8.0) for pancreatic digestive enzymes.
**Synergistic Action:** Augments CCK-driven pancreatic digestive enzyme output.
*Biliary System:*
**Direct Action on Cholangiocytes:** Stimulates epithelial cells of the liver bile ductules to secrete a watery, sodium bicarbonate-rich solution (more than doubling total bile volume post-meal).
*Gastric System:*
**Direct Action on Parietal & G Cells:** Inhibits gastric acid output by directly suppressing G-cell gastrin release and reducing parietal cell responsiveness to gastrin and histamine.
**Direct Action on Gastric Motility:** Inhibits stomach motility and delays gastric emptying (enterogastrone effect).
**Direct Action on Pyloric Sphincter:** Causes contraction of the pyloric sphincter, preventing premature duodenal filling.
*Endocrine & Vascular Systems:*
**Direct Action on Beta Cells:** Stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic islets.
**Direct Local Action:** Causes intestinal mucosal vasodilation, increasing blood flow during digestion.
Types / Isoforms
Native 27-amino acid peptide. Belongs to the secretin hormone family (includes GIP, VIP, Glucagon).
Regulation
*Negative Feedback Loop:* Acidic chyme stimulates S cells→ secretin release→ watery bicarbonate floods the duodenum→ neutralizes duodenal acid (pH > 5.0)→ shuts off secretin release.
Factors Affecting
*Increases:* Acidic chyme in duodenum (pH < 4.5) and protein digestion products.
*Decreases:* Duodenal neutralization (pH > 5.0) and somatostatin.
Clinical Correlates

*Diagnostic Secretin Test:* Used to assess exocrine pancreatic function and as a provocative test for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (secretin paradoxically increases serum gastrin in gastrinoma patients).
Characteristics
*Chemical Class:* Polypeptide hormone.
*Size / Structure:* Single chain of 42 amino acids. Belongs to the secretin family. Formerly termed Gastric Inhibitory Peptide.
Source
Produced by **K cells** located in the mucosa of the duodenum and jejunum.
Synthesis
Synthesized as a preprohormone precursor and cleaved into active 42-amino acid peptide.
Secretion
Stimulated by luminal glucose, amino acids, and fats (fatty acids, triglycerides) entering the upper small intestine.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
Cell-membrane GPCRs on pancreatic beta cells and gastric parietal cells.
Target Tissues
Pancreatic beta cells, pancreatic alpha cells, gastric parietal cells, and gastric smooth muscle.
Functions
*Endocrine & Metabolic System:*

**Primary Incretin Action:** Acts as a major physiological incretin that potently stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells in response to elevated blood glucose. Plasma insulin surges triggered by GIP match those produced by oral glucose ingestion (explaining why oral glucose elicits greater insulin release than intravenous glucose).
**Glucagon Modulation:** Inhibits glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells.
*Gastric System:*
**Direct Action on Stomach:** Weakly inhibits gastric acid secretion and gastric motility (enterogastrone effect).
Types / Isoforms
Native 42-amino acid polypeptide.
Regulation
Direct nutrient-sensing stimulation of K cells by luminal glucose and fat.
Factors Affecting
*Increases:* Luminal oral glucose, carbohydrates, intraduodenal fats, and amino acids.
*Decreases:* Fasting state and somatostatin.
Metabolism and Clearance
Inactivated rapidly in blood by the enzyme Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 (DPP-4).
Clinical Correlates

*Incretin Impairment & Diabetes:* Incretin responses are blunted in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. Incretin-based therapies (DPP-4 inhibitors) prevent degradation of endogenous GIP and GLP-1 to enhance insulin release and restore glucose control.
Characteristics
Polypeptide hormone derived from tissue-specific post-translational processing of proglucagon.
Source
Secreted by enteroendocrine **L cells** in the mucosa of the small intestine (jejunum, ileum) and colon. Also synthesized by central nervous system neurons in the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS).
Synthesis
Translated as preproglucagon (179 amino acids). In intestinal L cells and brain neurons, proglucagon is cleaved by prohormone convertase to yield GLP-1, GLP-2, glicentin, and oxyntomodulin.
Secretion
Secreted into blood following arrival of digested carbohydrates, fatty acids, and proteins in the intestinal lumen post-meal.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
Membrane GPCRs expressed on pancreatic beta cells, alpha cells, stomach, and hypothalamic brain circuits.
Target Tissues
Pancreatic beta and alpha cells, stomach, and brain (hypothalamic feeding centers).
Functions
*Endocrine & Metabolic System:*
**Potent Incretin Action:** Functions as the most potent physiological stimulator of insulin synthesis and secretion from pancreatic beta cells in response to elevated blood glucose.
**Glucagon Suppression:** Potently suppresses glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells.
*Gastric System:*
**Gastric Inhibitory Action:** Inhibits gastric acid secretion and delays gastric emptying.
*Central Nervous System & Satiety:*
**Anorexigenic Action:** Acts centrally on hypothalamic circuits to suppress appetite, promote satiety, and decrease food intake.
Types / Related Peptides
*GLP-1:* Primary active incretin peptide.
*GLP-2:* Co-secreted peptide; produced in the brain where it projects from the NTS to the dorsomedial nucleus of the hypothalamus to inhibit food intake.
Factors Affecting
*Increases:* Oral glucose, luminal fatty acids, and amino acids.
*Decreases:* Fasting and rapid enzymatic cleavage by DPP-4.
Metabolism and Clearance
Extremely short circulating half-life due to rapid cleavage and inactivation by Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 (DPP-4).
Clinical Correlates

*GLP-1 Receptor Agonists:* Synthetic DPP-4-resistant GLP-1 analogs used in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and obesity to enhance glucose-dependent insulin release, suppress glucagon, slow gastric emptying, and promote weight loss.
*DPP-4 Inhibitors:* Pharmacological agents that block DPP-4 enzymatic degradation, elevating endogenous circulating GLP-1 and GIP levels.
Characteristics
*Chemical Class:* Polypeptide hormone.
*Size / Structure:* Single chain of 28 amino acids. Belongs to the secretin family.
Properties
*Half-life:* Extremely short circulating half-life of 2 minutes.
Source
*Gland / Organ:* Secreted from mucosal cells and enteric neurons throughout the entire GI tract (from stomach to colon, with highest concentration in the colon).
*Neural Source:* Expressed in enteric nervous system (ENS) plexus neurons, autonomic nerves, blood, and central brain structures.
Synthesis
Formed from a large precursor, prepro-VIP, which encodes both VIP and PHM-27 (a closely related peptide).
Secretion
Secreted as an inhibitory neurotransmitter from non-adrenergic non-cholinergic (NANC) enteric nerve terminals upon local reflex stimulation.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
*Receptor Type & Location:* Cell-membrane GPCRs on enterocytes, vascular smooth muscle, intestinal smooth muscle, and parietal cells.
*Signaling Pathway & Second Messenger:* Activates membrane adenylyl cyclase to raise intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP).
*Downstream Effects:* cAMP stimulates active chloride (Cl⁻) and bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) secretion into the intestinal lumen via apical channels.
Target Tissues
Intestinal mucosal epithelial cells (enterocytes), vascular smooth muscle, intestinal smooth muscle/sphincters, salivary glands, and gastric parietal cells.
Functions
*Intestinal System:*
**Direct Action on Enterocytes:** Markedly increases intestinal fluid secretion exceptionally rich in electrolytes (Cl⁻,HCO₃⁻) and water.
**Direct Action on Intestinal Muscle:** Decreases GI motility and causes potent relaxation of intestinal smooth muscle and gastrointestinal sphincters.
*Cardiovascular System:*
**Direct Action on Blood Vessels:** Produces potent peripheral and splanchnic vasodilation, increasing local GI blood flow and reducing systemic blood pressure.
*Gastric System:*
**Direct Action on Stomach:** Inhibits gastric acid output and suppresses gastrin release.
*Exocrine Glands:*
**Potentiating Action:** Potentiates acetylcholine-driven salivary gland secretion.
Types / Isoforms
Native 28-amino acid peptide; co-translated with PHM-27.
Regulation
Regulated by intrinsic neural reflexes within the enteric nervous system. Suppressed by somatostatin.
Clinical Correlates

*VIPoma (Verner-Morrison Syndrome / WDHA Syndrome):* Rare neuroendocrine tumor secreting autonomous, excessive levels of VIP. Manifests as the **WDHA syndrome**: **W**atery **D**iarrhea (profuse, cholera-like secretory diarrhea), **H**ypokalemia, **A**chlorhydria/hypochlorhydria, and severe **H**ypotension due to profound vasodilation and volume depletion.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide hormone.
**Size/Structure:** Composed of a single chain of 22 amino acids.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Gastrointestinal tract.
**Specific Cell Type:** Secreted from Mo cells and enterochromaffin cells present in the mucosa of all parts of the gastrointestinal tract, except the esophagus and rectum.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Cell-membrane G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) located on enteric neurons.
Target Tissues
Enteric nervous system neurons and gastrointestinal smooth muscle cells.
Functions
**Gastrointestinal System:**
*Intestinal Smooth Muscle Contraction (Direct Action):* Causes contraction of intestinal smooth muscle, directly increasing overall gastrointestinal motility.

*Interdigestive Motility Regulation (Direct & Neural Action):* Serves as the primary physiological regulator of the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC / interdigestive myoelectric complex) that cleanses and regulates motility in the stomach and small intestine between meals. Phase III gastric MMC contractions are specifically driven by motilin release mediated via the vagus nerve.
*Peristaltic Enhancement (Direct Action):* Enhances small intestinal propulsive peristalsis during food processing.
Regulation
**Cyclic Interdigestive Axis:** Secretion occurs in cyclic bursts during fasting/interdigestive states to initiate MMC cycles.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion / Action:** Fasting / interdigestive state, starving, thirsty state, and vagal nerve stimulation.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion / Action:** Ingestion of a meal and somatostatin.
Clinical Correlates

**Therapeutic Motilin Agonism:** Erythromycin (a macrolide antibiotic) and its derivatives bind to and activate motilin receptors, acting as motilin agonists to facilitate intestinal motility in patients suffering from gastrointestinal hypomotility (e.g., gastroparesis).
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide hormone.
**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 28 amino acids.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Gastrointestinal tract (secreted mainly from the stomach).
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Location:** Receptors located on arcuate nucleus neurons in the hypothalamus and somatotrophs in the anterior pituitary gland.
Target Tissues
Arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary gland (somatotrophs).
Functions
**Central Nervous & Feeding System:**
*Orexigenic Appetite Stimulation (Direct Central Action):* Acts as a potent orexigenic agent on the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus to stimulate hunger and increase food intake.
**Anterior Pituitary / Somatotrophic System:**

*Growth Hormone Secretion (Direct Endocrine Action):* Directly stimulates the synthesis and secretion of growth hormone (GH / somatotropin) from somatotrophs in the anterior pituitary gland. Functions as an important hypothalamic/gastrointestinal growth hormone-releasing factor (GHRF).
Regulation
**Nutritional Pre-Meal Axis:** Governed by acute nutritional status and feeding intervals; surges prior to meal initiation.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion / Action:** Hunger state / pre-meal state, starvation, acute hypoglycemia, low blood free fatty acids, and elevated plasma amino acids (e.g., arginine).
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide hormone.
**Size/Structure:** Polypeptide displaying structural resemblance to Neuropeptide Y (NPY) and Pancreatic Polypeptide (PP).
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Distal gastrointestinal tract.
**Specific Location:** Secreted from mucosal endocrine cells of the small intestine (jejunum and ileum) and colon.
Target Tissues
Gastric parietal/smooth muscle cells and hypothalamic feeding centers.
Functions
**Gastrointestinal System:**

*Gastric Secretory & Motility Inhibition (Direct Action):* Potently inhibits gastric acid secretion and gastric motility, acting as an effective physiological enterogastrone / gastric inhibitory peptide.
**Central Nervous & Feeding System:**
*Anorexigenic Satiety Induction (Direct Central Action):* Acts on central hypothalamic circuits to inhibit food intake and suppress feeding (exerting the opposite effect of structurally related NPY).
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion:** Arrival and presence of dietary lipids/fat in the jejunum and small intestine.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide hormone.
**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 15 amino acids.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Small intestine.
**Specific Cell Type:** Produced and secreted by Paneth cells (endocrine cells located in the crypts of Lieberkühn) of the small intestine.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action

**Receptor Type & Location:** Transmembrane guanylin receptors (membrane-bound guanylyl cyclase) located on intestinal enterocytes, as well as cells in the kidneys, liver, and female reproductive tract.
**Signaling Pathway & Second Messenger:** Binds guanylyl cyclase, markedly increasing intracellular **cyclic GMP (cGMP)**.

**Downstream Effects:** Intracellular cGMP activates cGMP-dependent protein kinases and phosphatases, directly opening and increasing the activity of apical chloride channels to drive active chloride ion transport.
Target Tissues
Intestinal mucosal epithelial cells (enterocytes), kidneys, liver, and female reproductive tract tissue.
Functions
**Intestinal System:**

*Intestinal Chloride & Fluid Secretion (Direct Action):* Stimulates active secretion of chloride ions into the intestinal lumen, driving passive water movement and regulating fluid balance across the intestinal mucosa.
**Renal, Hepatic & Reproductive Systems:**

*Multi-Organ Fluid Integration (Direct Action):* Controls fluid movement in renal, hepatic, and female reproductive epithelia, specifically integrating fluid homeostasis between the intestine and the kidneys.
Clinical Correlates

**Pathogenic Diarrhea (E. coli Enterotoxins):** Heat-stable enterotoxins produced by certain pathogenic strains of *E. coli* share structural homology with guanylin. These enterotoxins bind and hyperactivate guanylin receptors on intestinal enterocytes, producing massive cGMP surges, uncontrolled chloride and fluid secretion into the lumen, and severe watery diarrhea.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Acid protease enzyme / glycoprotein hormone.
**Size/Structure:** Glycoprotein with a molecular weight of 37,326; active form consists of 340 amino acids.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Kidneys (Juxtaglomerular Apparatus / JGA).
**Specific Cell Types:**

*Juxtaglomerular (JG) Cells:* Modified vascular smooth muscle cells with an epithelioid appearance containing dense secretory granules, located in the walls of the afferent arterioles immediately proximal to the glomeruli.
*Lacis Cells:* Extraglomerular mesangial cells located in the triangular space between afferent/efferent arterioles and macula densa.
Synthesis

**Precursor Processing:** Synthesized on rough ER as **preprorenin** (406 amino acids)→ cleaved to **prorenin** (383 amino acids)→ processed and stored in secretory granules of JG cells as active **renin** (340 amino acids).
Secretion
**Mechanism:** Exocytosis of secretory granules into renal blood circulation and local renal interstitium.
**Stimuli for Release:**
*Renal Baroreceptor Mechanism:* Decreased renal arterial blood pressure or renal perfusion pressure sensed by pressure-sensitive baroreceptors in JG cells.
*Macula Densa Mechanism:* Decreased sodium chloride delivery/concentration at the macula densa cells of the early distal tubule.
*Sympathetic Neural Mechanism:* Increased renal sympathetic nerve discharge acting directly on JG cellβ_1-adrenergic receptors.
*Humoral / Systemic Stimuli:* Circulating catecholamines, prostaglandins, hypovolemia/hemorrhage, dehydration, standing posture, heart failure, and liver cirrhosis.
Transport

Most secreted renin enters renal venous blood to circulate throughout the systemic circulation (persisting in blood for 30 minutes to 1 hour); small amounts remain locally in renal interstitium to govern intrarenal hemodynamics.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action (Substrate Specificity)
**Substrate / Target:** Renin acts as a specific circulating protease on **angiotensinogen** (renin substrate; a 453-amino acidα_2-globulin synthesized by the liver).

**Enzymatic Reaction:** Cleaves angiotensinogen to release the decapeptide **Angiotensin I**. Angiotensin I is subsequently converted by Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) in pulmonary and vascular endothelium into the octapeptide **Angiotensin II**.
Target Tissues
Circulating plasma angiotensinogen. (Downstream actions mediated via Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle, adrenal cortex, renal tubules, brain, and pituitary).
Functions
**Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) Initiation:**

*Angiotensin I Cleavage (Direct Enzymatic Action):* Catalyzes the rate-limiting conversion of liver-derived angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, initiating the RAAS cascade to restore blood volume and blood pressure.
**Downstream Systemic Effects (Mediated via Generated Angiotensin II):**

*Arteriolar Vasoconstriction:* Angiotensin II causes potent systemic arteriolar vasoconstriction (8 times more potent than norepinephrine), rapidly elevating total peripheral resistance and arterial blood pressure.

*Adrenal Aldosterone Secretion:* Angiotensin II acts as the primary physiological stimulus on the adrenal zona glomerulosa to synthesize and release aldosterone, driving renal sodium and water reabsorption.

*Renal Glomerular & Tubular Autoregulation:* Angiotensin II selectively constricts efferent arterioles to maintain glomerular filtration rate (GFR) during renal hypoperfusion and directly increases sodium/water reabsorption in proximal convoluted tubules.

*Central & Neuroendocrine Activation:* Angiotensin II acts centrally to stimulate dipsogenesis (thirst), activate the brainstem vasomotor center to increase sympathetic outflow, and stimulate pituitary secretion of ADH and ACTH.
Regulation
**Negative Feedback Loops:**
*Hemodynamic & Electrolyte Feedback:* Elevated blood pressure, increased ECF volume, and increased sodium delivery to the macula densa suppress renin secretion.
*Direct Hormonal Feedback:* Angiotensin II and ADH directly inhibit JG cell renin release.
*Dietary Salt Adaptation:* High dietary salt intake expands ECF volume and suppresses renin/Angiotensin II; low salt intake stimulates renin output to conserve salt and maintain pressure.
Factors Affecting

**Factors Increasing Secretion:** Hypotension, hypovolemia (hemorrhage), hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, dehydration, standing posture, renal artery constriction/stenosis, heart failure, liver cirrhosis, sympathetic stimulation, prostaglandins, and psychological depression.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Hypertension, hypernatremia, ECF volume expansion, Angiotensin II, ADH, andβ-adrenergic antagonists.
Clinical Correlates
**Primary Reninism (Renin-Secreting Tumor):** Tumor of the juxtaglomerular cells secreting autonomous, excessive renin, causing severe hypertension and secondary hyperaldosteronism.

**Primary Aldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome):** High aldosterone from an adrenal adenoma expands ECF volume and elevates blood pressure, causing **feedback suppression of plasma renin concentration** (a key diagnostic criterion).

**Secondary Hyperaldosteronism:** High circulating renin levels driven by hypovolemia or renal hypoperfusion in congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, or renal artery stenosis.

**Bartter Syndrome:** Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia resulting from mutations in the renalNa⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter gene, causing massive renin secretion, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalemic alkalosis, and hypercalciuria without hypertension or edema.

**Goldblatt Hypertension:** Experimental or clinical stenosis/constriction of the renal artery causes acute renal ischemia, triggering large surges in renin release that drive severe Angiotensin II-mediated renovascular hypertension.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Glycoprotein hormone.
**Size/Structure:** Polypeptide containing 165 amino acids attached to 4 oligosaccharide chains required for biological activity; molecular weight of approximately 34,000.
Properties
**Solubility & Half-Life:** Water-soluble glycoprotein. Circulating half-life is approximately **5 hours**.
**Biological Requirement:** Carbohydrate/oligosaccharide moieties are strictly necessary for its physiological activity in vivo.
Source
**Gland/Organ & Specific Cells:**

*Renal Source (85–90% of total):* Produced primarily by **fibroblast-like interstitial cells** surrounding the tubules in the peritubular capillary bed of the renal cortex and outer medulla. Minor contributions originate from juxtaglomerular cells and extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells.
*Hepatic Source (10–15% of total):* Produced in the liver by nonparenchymal Kupffer cells and perivenous hepatocytes.
Synthesis & Molecular Induction
**Hypoxia-Inducible Factor-1 (HIF-1) Pathway:**
Renal tissue hypoxia suppresses HIF hydroxylases, preventing degradation of theα subunit of **Hypoxia-Inducible Factor-1 (HIF-1)**.
α andβ subunits dimerize to form active HIF-1 transcription factor.
HIF-1 binds to the *hypoxia response element* residing in the erythropoietin gene in renal cortical fibroblasts, driving mRNA transcription and rapid EPO protein synthesis.
Secretion

**Stimuli for Release:** Decreased tissue oxygenation / tissue hypoxia (induced by anemia, low blood volume, high altitude, lung disease, or poor renal blood flow), catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine), and prostaglandins.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Specific erythropoietin receptors belonging to the **cytokine receptor superfamily**, expressed on erythroid progenitor and precursor membranes in bone marrow.
**Signaling Pathway:**
EPO binding induces receptor dimerization and activates associated intrinsic/cytosolic tyrosine kinases.
Initiates a phosphorylation cascade of serine and threonine kinases, culminating in the activation of **Janus kinase 2 (JAK-2 protein)**.
JAK-2 and downstream signaling translocate to the nucleus to alter gene transcription, promoting cell survival, proliferation, and maturation.
Target Tissues
Bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells, erythroid progenitor cells (BFU-E and CFU-E), and early erythroid precursor cells (pronormoblasts and normoblasts).
Functions
**Erythroid & Hematopoietic System (Chief Mediator of Functional Feedback):**
*Stem Cell Commitment:* Acts on uncommitted hematopoietic stem cells to promote their transformation and differentiation toward the erythroid cell lineage.

*Progenitor Proliferation:* Acts specifically on progenitor cells to stimulate **Burst-Forming Units-Erythroid (BFU-E)** and **Colony-Forming Units-Erythroid (CFU-E)** to proliferate and form pronormoblasts.
*Mitotic Acceleration:* Decreases the cell cycle length of erythroid precursor cells, enhancing the rate of mitotic divisions.
*Normoblast Maturation:* Facilitates the structural and functional maturation of normoblasts into reticulocytes.
*Hemoglobin Synthesis:* Enhances rate of hemoglobin synthesis within developing normoblasts.
*Reticulocyte Release:* Stimulates early release of reticulocytes from the bone marrow sinusoids into the circulating blood.
Regulation

**Functional Oxygenation Feedback Loop:** Governed by the balance between tissue oxygen demand and supply. Hypoxia triggers HIF-1 and EPO surges; relief of tissue hypoxia leads to normoxic HIF-1 degradation by HIF hydroxylases, shutting off EPO synthesis.
**Hormonal Regulation of EPO Production:**
*Stimulatory Hormones:* Androgens (increase EPO production and directly stimulate bone marrow), Thyroxine, Prolactin, ACTH, Epinephrine, Norepinephrine, Cortisol, and Growth Hormone.
*Inhibitory Hormones:* Estrogen directly inhibits EPO production and decreases stem cell responsiveness to EPO (explaining lower RBC counts in females and reduced incidence of Monge's disease).
**Chemical Modulators:** Adenosine antagonists (e.g., theophylline) inhibit EPO secretion.
Metabolism and Clearance
Primary site of inactivation and clearance is the liver. Biological circulating half-life is approximately **5 hours**.
Clinical Correlates

**Renal Disease Anemia:** Chronic kidney disease or surgical nephrectomy destroys renal peritubular interstitial cells, eliminating ~90% of EPO production. The remaining 10% liver output supports only one-third of normal RBC production, resulting in severe chronic anemia. Managed therapeutically with recombinant human erythropoietin.

**High Altitude Acclimatization & Polycythemia:** Prolonged exposure to low atmosphericPO₂ at high altitude stimulates sustained EPO release, raising hematocrit from 40% to ~60% and hemoglobin from 15 to ~20 g/dL.

**Chronic Mountain Sickness (Monge's Disease):** Pathological extreme polycythemia resulting from chronic altitude hypoxia; significantly less common in females due to estrogenic inhibition of EPO output.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Steroid derivative / Secosteroid hormone.
**Identifying Features:** Hormonally active, most potent biological form of Vitamin D₃ (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol).
Properties
**Solubility:** Lipid-soluble steroid derivative.
**Storage:** Vitamin D is stored as 25-hydroxycholecalciferol in the liver for many months for future use.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Kidneys (mitochondria of proximal tubules).
**Precursor Molecules:**
**7-dehydrocholesterol** (present in skin).
**Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D₃)** (formed in skin via UV irradiation or acquired from diet).
**25-hydroxycholecalciferol** (formed in liver).
Synthesis
**Key Steps & Enzymes:**
*Skin Phase:* Irradiation of **7-dehydrocholesterol** by ultraviolet rays from sunlight forms **Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D₃)**.
*Liver Phase:* Cholecalciferol is converted to **25-hydroxycholecalciferol** in the liver (limited by negative feedback inhibition to conserve storage).

*Renal Activation Step (Rate-Limiting):* In the mitochondria of renal proximal tubules, **1α-hydroxylase** hydroxylates 25-hydroxycholecalciferol at the 1-position to form active **1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (Calcitriol)**. *Note: Requires Parathyroid Hormone (PTH).*
Secretion / Activation Stimuli
Primary stimuli: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH), low plasma calcium concentration, low plasma phosphate.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Nuclear **Vitamin D Receptors (VDR)** present in nuclei of target cells. Contains hormone-binding and DNA-binding domains.
**Affinity:** Affinity for calcitriol is roughly **1000 times** greater than for 25-hydroxycholecalciferol.
**Mechanism & Downstream Effects:**
Binds nuclear VDR, altering DNA transcription and mRNA translation.
Upregulates synthesis of **Calbindin** (a calcium-binding protein), calcium-stimulated ATPase, and alkaline phosphatase in intestinal enterocytes.
Target Tissues
Intestinal epithelium (brush border), bones (osteoblasts, osteoclasts), kidneys (tubular cells), and parathyroid chief cells.
Functions
**Gastrointestinal System (Direct Actions):**

*Intestinal Calcium Absorption (Direct Action):* Promotes intestinal calcium absorption by increasing the formation of **calbindin** in intestinal epithelial cells over ~2 days. Calbindin transports calcium across the brush border into the cytoplasm, followed by basolateral facilitated diffusion into blood.
*Epithelial Enzyme Activation (Direct Action):* Stimulates brush-border calcium-stimulated ATPase and epithelial alkaline phosphatase to facilitate calcium transport.
*Intestinal Phosphate Absorption (Direct & Indirect Action):* Enhances epithelial phosphate flux across intestinal mucosa directly and secondarily via calcium transport mediation.
**Skeletal System (Direct & Permissive Actions):**
*Bone Calcification / Mineralization (Direct Action at Physiological Doses):* Promotes bone calcification and enhances osteoblastic mineralization independent of intestinal absorption.

*Bone Resorption (Permissive/Synergistic Action with PTH at Extreme Doses):* Extreme quantities cause bone resorption. In the absence of calcitriol, the effect of PTH in causing bone resorption is greatly reduced or prevented.
**Renal System (Direct Actions):**

*Tubular Reabsorption (Direct Weak Action):* Increases calcium and phosphate reabsorption by renal tubular epithelial cells (thick ascending limb and distal tubules), reducing urinary calcium and phosphate loss.
**Anti-Aging & Cellular Integration:**
*Interaction withα-Klotho:* Acts partly through **α-Klotho** anti-aging protein to facilitate membrane localization of calcium and phosphate reabsorption proteins (TRPV5, Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase).
Types / Forms
**Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D₃):** Inactive skin precursor.
**25-Hydroxycholecalciferol:** Circulating storage form (<1/1000th biological activity).
**1,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol (Calcitriol):** Fully active steroid hormone.
Regulation
**PTH Control:** Conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to calcitriol in proximal tubules requires PTH.
**Calcium Feedback Loop:** Plasma calcium inverse relationship: hypocalcemia (<9–10 mg/dL) stimulates PTH and calcitriol formation; hypercalcemia suppresses PTH and depresses calcitriol formation.
**FGF-23 / Klotho Axis:** Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 (FGF-23) inhibits 1α-hydroxylase, reducing calcitriol levels.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Formation:** PTH, hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, pregnancy, and lactation (maternal calcitriol surges to maintain calcium for fetal bone and milk).
**Factors Decreasing Formation:** Hypercalcemia, FGF-23, Klotho deficiency, and chronic renal disease / kidney damage.
Metabolism and Clearance
Liver stores 25-hydroxycholecalciferol for months. Inactivated by 24-hydroxylation in kidneys/liver.
Clinical Correlates
**Secondary Hyperparathyroidism:** Caused by chronic renal disease where damaged kidneys fail to form calcitriol, leading to hypocalcemia, osteomalacia, and compensatory PTH elevation.
**Renal Rickets / Osteomalacia:** Prolonged kidney damage prevents calcitriol synthesis, causing bone demineralization.
**Vitamin D-Resistant Rickets:** Congenital hypophosphatemia caused by reduced renal tubular phosphate reabsorption; requires treatment with phosphate compounds rather than Vitamin D.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide hormone.
**Size/Structure:** Single chain of 28 amino acids.
Properties
**Solubility:** Water-soluble peptide.
**Storage:** Stored in secretory granules within atrial cardiac muscle fibers.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Heart (specifically **cardiac atrial muscle fibers / atrial myocytes**).
Secretion
**Primary Stimulus:** Increased stretch of cardiac atria resulting from excess blood volume, ECF expansion, increased venous return, or hypertension.
**Mechanism:** Exocytosis from atrial myocyte granules into circulation.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action

**Receptor Type & Signaling:** Binds membrane natriuretic peptide receptors on target cells (e.g., vascular smooth muscle, renal tubules), activating guanylyl cyclase to increase cytosolic **cyclic GMP (cGMP)**.
Target Tissues
Kidneys (afferent/efferent arterioles, collecting ducts, JG cells), vascular smooth muscle, adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa), and posterior pituitary.
Functions
**Renal & Electrolyte System (Direct Actions):**

*Glomerular Filtration Rate Increase (Direct Action):* Causes dilation of renal afferent arterioles and constriction of efferent arterioles, raising glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and increasing GFR.

*Inhibition of Tubular Sodium Reabsorption (Direct Action):* Inhibits NaCl and water reabsorption in late distal tubules and medullary collecting ducts, producing profound **natriuresis and diuresis**.
*Suppression of Renin Release (Direct Action):* Decreases renin secretion from juxtaglomerular (JG) cells, suppressing Angiotensin II formation.
**Cardiovascular & Hemodynamic System (Direct Actions):**
*Systemic Vasodilation:* Relaxes vascular smooth muscle, producing vasodilation and decreasing systemic blood pressure.
*ECF & Blood Volume Reduction:* Reduces total ECF volume, blood volume, and cardiac venous return to relieve volume overload on the heart.
**Endocrine System (Direct & Indirect Actions):**
*Adrenal Aldosterone Inhibition (Direct Action):* Acts on zona glomerulosa cells of the adrenal cortex to inhibit aldosterone synthesis and secretion.
*ADH Release Suppression (Indirect Action):* Signals central structures to decrease posterior pituitary secretion of ADH, promoting renal water excretion.
Types / Related Peptides
**ANP:** Native 28-amino acid cardiac peptide.
**Urodilatin:** Related 32-amino acid polypeptide secreted by renal distal tubules/collecting ducts that acts locally to cause natriuresis.
Regulation
**Direct Atrial Volume Feedback Loop:** ECF volume expansion→ atrial stretch→ ANP release→ natriuresis/diuresis→ ECF volume returns to normal→ shuts off atrial stretch.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion:** Excess blood volume, increased venous return, high dietary sodium/water intake, hypertension, atrial stretch, and hypervolemia.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Hypovolemia, dehydration, hemorrhage, and decreased atrial fill/pressure.
Clinical Correlates

**Aldosterone Escape Phenomenon:** Excess aldosterone-induced salt/water reabsorption expands ECF volume→ increases venous return and stretches cardiac atria→ triggers ANP release→ profound natriuresis and diuresis that returns ECF volume toward normal.
**Heart Failure Biomarker:** Chronic atrial distension in congestive heart failure causes marked elevation of plasma ANP to compensate for volume overload.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Cytokine-related protein / Polypeptide hormone.
Properties
**Solubility:** Water-soluble polypeptide.
**Storage & Secretion Rate:** Secretion rate is directly proportional to total white adipose tissue mass (degree of adiposity).
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Adipose tissue (specifically **white fat cells / white adipocytes**).
Transport
Circulates in plasma unbound and bound to soluble leptin receptors; crosses the blood-brain barrier via receptor-mediated transport.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Type & Location:** Cell-surface **Leptin Receptor (Ob-R)**, a member of the cytokine receptor superfamily, located heavily in the **arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus** and other tissues.

**Signaling Pathway:** Homodimerization activates associated **Janus kinase 2 (JAK2)**→ phosphorylates **STAT3** (Signal Transducers and Activators of Transcription)→ STAT3 translocates to the nucleus to bind response elements and activate mRNA transcription. JAK2 also activates rapid intracellular enzyme cascades.
Target Tissues
Hypothalamus (arcuate nucleus, PVN, TRH neurons), brown adipose tissue, thyroid axis, adrenal cortex, and gonads.
Functions
**Central Nervous System / Feeding & Energy Balance:**

*Anorexigenic Satiety Induction (Direct Central Action):* Acts on the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus to decrease appetite and food intake. Suppresses orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons and activates anorexigenic POMC/CART neurons.
*Energy Expenditure Stimulation (Direct Central Action):* Acts on hypothalamic centers to increase overall peripheral energy expenditure.
*Sympathetic Outflow Activation (Direct Action):* Stimulates central autonomic centers to increase sympathetic nervous system activity.
**Thermoregulatory & Adipose System:**
*Uncoupling Protein Activation (Direct/Autonomic Action):* Increases the activity of **Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP-1 / thermogenin)** in brown adipose tissue cells, driving non-shivering thermogenesis.
**Reproductive & Developmental Systems:**
*Puberty Onset Trigger (Permissive Action):* Signals body fat sufficiency to the hypothalamus to regulate the normal timing and onset of puberty.
**Endocrine System:**
*Thyroid Function Stimulation (Direct Action):* Acts on hypothalamic TRH neurons (directly and via POMC/NPY modulation) to stimulate TRH, TSH, and thyroid hormone output during fed states.
*Glucocorticoid Output Modulation:* Regulates baseline secretion of glucocorticoids (cortisol) from the adrenal cortex.
Regulation
**Lipostatic Feedback Axis:**
*High Leptin (Obesity / Fed State):* Decreases food intake, increases energy expenditure, and increases sympathetic activity.

*Low Leptin (Starvation / Fasting):* Decreases POMC and increases NPY/AgRP, directly decreasing TRH/TSH/thyroid output (conserving energy), increasing food intake, decreasing energy expenditure, and increasing parasympathetic activity.
Factors Affecting
**Factors Increasing Secretion:** Obesity, increased white adipose tissue mass, feeding, insulin, and glucocorticoids.
**Factors Decreasing Secretion:** Starvation, fasting, weight loss, and prolonged calorie restriction.
Clinical Correlates
**Leptin Resistance in Obesity:** In human obesity, circulating leptin levels are high, but central hypothalamic responsiveness is blunted (leptin resistance), preventing normal satiety.
**Congenital Leptin Deficiency:** Loss of leptin signaling produces severe hyperphagia, morbid obesity, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
A. Adiponectin
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Complement-related protein / Adipokine.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Adipose tissue (**white adipocytes**).
Target Tissues
Liver, skeletal muscle, vascular endothelium, and hypothalamus.
Functions
**Metabolic System (Direct Actions):**
*Insulin Sensitization:* Enhances insulin sensitivity in liver and skeletal muscle, promoting glucose uptake and fatty acid oxidation.
*Anti-Diabetic Action:* Decreases overall insulin resistance (acts reciprocally to leptin).
**Cardiovascular & Inflammatory System (Direct Actions):**
*Anti-Inflammatory & Anti-Atherogenic:* Protects against chronic systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and Metabolic Syndrome (Met-S).
Regulation & Factors Affecting
Secretion is **inversely** related to body fat mass.
*Decreased by:* Obesity, visceral fat accumulation, TNF-α, and IL-6.
*Increased by:* Weight loss, exercise, and PPAR-γ agonists.
Clinical Correlates
**Hypoadiponectinemia:** Reduced plasma adiponectin is strongly associated with obesity, Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (NIDDM), insulin resistance, and Metabolic Syndrome.
B. Resistin
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Cysteine-rich peptide / Adipokine.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** Adipose tissue (white adipocytes and intra-adipose monocytes/macrophages).
Target Tissues
Liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue.
Functions
**Metabolic System (Direct Actions):**
*Insulin Resistance Induction:* Antagonizes insulin signaling pathways in liver and muscle, impairing glucose uptake and elevating blood glucose.
**Inflammatory System:**
*Pro-Inflammatory Signaling:* Modulates chronic systemic inflammation in obesity.
Factors Affecting & Clinical Correlates
*Increased by:* Obesity, visceral adiposity, and inflammatory cytokines.
*Clinical Significance:* Markedly elevated in NIDDM (Type 2 DM) and obesity, serving as a key molecular link between obesity and insulin resistance.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Polypeptide hormones / Thymic humoral factors.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** **Thymus gland** (a primary lymphoid organ located in the anterior mediastinum).
**Specific Cell Type:** Thymic epithelial cells and Hassall's corpuscles.
Target Tissues
Bone marrow-derived prethymic cells, uncommitted pre-T cells, cytotoxic T cells, suppressor T cells, helper T cells, and mononuclear phagocytes.
Functions
1. Thymulin
*T Cell Function Enhancement (Direct Action):* Enhances the functional differentiation and activity of various types of T cells, **specially suppressor T cells**.
2. Thymopoietin
*Cytotoxic T Cell Production (Direct Action):* Stimulates the production and maturation of **cytotoxic T cells**.
*T Cell Activity Balance (Synergistic Action):* Combined action with thymulin allows precise operational balance between cytotoxic and suppressor T cell activities.
3. Thymosin
*Lymphocyte & Antibody Production (Thymosinα-1):* **Thymosinα-1** stimulates lymphocyte production and drives plasma cell antibody production.
*Mononuclear Phagocyte Production (Thymosinβ-4):* **Thymosinβ-4** is produced by mononuclear phagocytes to modulate immune responses.
4. Thymic Humoral Factor
*T Helper & Suppressor Proliferation:* Controls the multiplication and expansion of helper and suppressor T cells.
**Overall Development of Acquired Immunity:** The epithelial cells guide prethymic cells to mature into immunocompetent T cells capable of cellular immunity and immunological tolerance.
Factors Affecting / Age-Related Involution
High activity during childhood; undergoes age-dependent thymic involution post-puberty, though functional stroma persists in adult life.
Clinical Correlates
**Effects of Early Thymectomy:** Thymectomy in young animals/infants leads to severe depletion of T cells, loss of cellular immunity, and fatal immunodeficiency within a few months.
Characteristics
**Chemical Class:** Amine / Biogenic indoleamine derived from tryptophan. Known as the **"hormone of the night"**.
Properties
**Solubility:** Lipid-soluble amine.
**Storage & Circulation:** Secreted into circulation from fenestrated capillaries of the pineal gland; measured in blood or saliva.
Source
**Gland/Organ:** **Pineal gland (Epiphysis cerebri)**.
**Specific Cell Type:** Pinealocytes.
**Precursor Molecule:** Amino acid **Tryptophan**.
Synthesis
**Key Steps & Enzymes:**
**Tryptophan**→ 5-Hydroxytryptophan→ **Serotonin (5-HT)**.
Serotonin→ (catalyzed by rate-limiting enzyme **Arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase [AANAT] / Serotonin N-acetyltransferase**)→ N-Acetylserotonin.
N-Acetylserotonin→ (catalyzed by Hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase [HIOMT])→ **Melatonin**.
Secretion

**Diurnal / Circadian Pattern:** Secreted in a strict 24-hour diurnal rhythm independent of lifestyle. Secretion surges dramatically during environmental darkness/nighttime (evening and first half of night) and is suppressed by daylight/photic stimulation.

**Neural Mechanism:** Photic stimulation of retina→ retinohypothalamic tract→ activates Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN)→ controls superior cervical ganglion (SCG) sympathetic output→ noradrenergic postganglionic terminals release Norepinephrine→ acts on **β-adrenergic receptors** on pinealocytes→ increases **cAMP**→ activates AANAT→ drives melatonin release into fenestrated capillaries.
Receptors and Mechanism of Action
**Receptor Types & Locations:** G-protein coupled receptors **MT₁** and **MT₂**.
**MT₁:** Found mainly in the SCN, retina, and pars tuberalis of the anterior pituitary gland.
**MT₂:** Found in the retina and SCN.
Target Tissues
Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of hypothalamus, brain reticular activating system, retina, anterior pituitary gland, and gonads / HPG axis.
Functions
**Central Nervous System / Circadian Rhythm & Sleep Synchronization:**
*Biological Clock Resetting (Direct Action via MT₁/MT₂):* Acts directly on SCN receptors to reset and synchronize biological clock rhythms with light-dark cycles.
*Sleep-Wake Cycle Control (Direct Action):* Released into circulation to act on brain reticular activating neurons, mediating sleep induction and sleep-wake rhythms.
**Reproductive & Developmental Systems:**
*Seasonal Reproductive Synchronization:* Synchronizes animal reproductive cycles in relation to environmental light/seasons.
*HPG Axis Regulation & Puberty Timing:* Regulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and gonadotropic hormone secretion, controlling the timing and onset of puberty.
**Endocrine System:**
*Thyroid & GnRH Bioavailability Modulation:* Regulates thyroid hormone bioavailability, which in turn modulates GnRH secretions.
Regulation

**Retinohypothalamic Photic Loop:** Daylight photic stimulation of retina activates SCN, suppressing pineal sympathetic output and inhibiting AANAT/melatonin. Darkness removes inhibition→ noradrenergicβ-receptor activation→ cAMP surge→ AANAT activation→ nighttime melatonin surge.
Factors Affecting
*Increases Secretion:* Darkness / night, SCG sympathetic activation, noradrenergicβ-agonists, and elevated cAMP.
*Decreases Secretion:* Daylight / photic retinal exposure,β-adrenergic blockers, and aging.
Clinical Correlates
**Dim Light Melatonin Onset (DLMO):** Diagnostic technique measuring salivary or blood melatonin to assess circadian clock alignment, phase shifts, and sleep disturbances in humans.
**Melatonin Therapy:** Used therapeutically for jet lag, shift-work disorders, and circadian sleep-wake cycle disturbances.
